<!-- theorem-1: body_md -->
\label{t.main}
For every $t\geqslant0$ and $q\in\mathcal Q_2^{\mathscr{S}}$, we have 
\begin{equation}
\label{e.main.1}
\lim_{N\to\infty}\overline F_N(t,q)=\sup_{p\in\mathcal Q_{\infty,\leqslant\lambda_\infty}^{\mathscr{S}}}\ \inf_{q'\in\mathcal Q_\infty^{\mathscr{S}}}\ \mathcal J_{t,q}(q',p).
\end{equation}
Moreover, denoting this limit by $f(t,q)$, the function $f$ is the Lipschitz viscosity solution to
\begin{equation}
\label{e.main.hj}
\begin{cases}
\partial_t f-\displaystyle\int_0^1\xi\left(\partial_q f\right)=0, &\text{on }\mathbb{R}_+\times\mathcal Q_2^{\mathscr{S}},\\
f(0,\cdot)=\psi, &\text{on }\mathcal Q_2^{\mathscr{S}}.
\end{cases}
\end{equation}
In particular, $f(t,0)$ is the limit of the quantity in~\eqref{e.def.FN.delta0}.
<!-- end theorem-1 -->
<!-- proposition-1: body_md -->
\label{p.F_N_smooth}
For every $N\in\mathbb{N}$, $t,t'\geqslant0$, and $q,q'\in\mathcal Q_\infty^{\mathscr{S}}$,
\begin{equation}
    \left|\overline F_N(t,q)-\overline F_N(t',q')\right|\leqslant |q-q'|_{L^1}+|t-t'|\sup_{a\in\prod_s[-\lambda_{N,s},\lambda_{N,s}]}|\xi(a)|.
    \label{e.F_N_Lipschitz}
\end{equation}
In particular, $\overline F_N$ extends uniquely by continuity to $\mathbb{R}_+\times\mathcal Q_1^{\mathscr{S}}$, and~\eqref{e.F_N_Lipschitz} remains valid there. The restriction of $\overline F_N$ to $\mathbb{R}_+\times\mathcal Q_2^{\mathscr{S}}$ is Gateaux differentiable in $q$, with
\begin{equation}
    \partial_q\overline F_N(t,q)\in\mathcal Q_{\infty,\leqslant\lambda_N}^{\mathscr{S}},
    \qquad (t,q)\in\mathbb{R}_+\times\mathcal Q_2^{\mathscr{S}},
    \label{e.bounds.der.FN}
\end{equation}
and, for every $q\in\mathcal Q_\infty^{\mathscr{S}}$ and $\kappa\in L^2([0,1);\mathbb{R}^{\mathscr{S}})$,
\begin{equation}
    \left\langle\kappa,\partial_q\overline F_N(t,q)\right\rangle_{L^2}=\mathbb{E}\left\langle\kappa(\alpha\wedge\alpha')\cdot R_N(\sigma,\sigma')\right\rangle_{N,t,q}.
    \label{e.def.der.FN}
\end{equation}
<!-- end proposition-1 -->
<!-- proof-1: body_md -->
This is~\cite[Proposition~5.1]{chen2025free}, in the diagonal multi-species form of~\cite[Proposition~4.1]{chen2024ms}, and we only explain why the argument applies to the spherical reference measure. The only property of $P_N$ that it uses is the bound $|R_{N,s}(\sigma,\sigma')|\leqslant\lambda_{N,s}$, which follows from the identity $R_N(\sigma,\sigma)=\lambda_N$ and the Cauchy--Schwarz inequality; in particular, $|R_N(\sigma,\sigma')|\leqslant|\lambda_N|\leqslant1$ for the Euclidean norm, since the entries of $\lambda_N$ are nonnegative and sum to~$1$. The membership of $\partial_q\overline F_N(t,q)$ in the cone of nonnegative nondecreasing paths is obtained there by duality from a monotonicity property of $\overline F_N(t,\cdot)$, see \cite[Proposition~3.8]{mourrat2023free}, whose proof only assumes that the reference measure is supported in the ball of radius $\sqrt N$, as is $P_N$.
<!-- end proof-1 -->
<!-- proposition-2: body_md -->
\label{p.semi-concave}
There exists a constant $C<\infty$, depending only on $\xi$, such that, for every $N\in\mathbb{N}$, $c\in(0,1]$, $t\geqslant0$, $q,q'\in\mathcal Q_{\uparrow,c}^{\mathscr{S}}$ with $ 
\accentset{\mbox{\large\bfseries .}}{q}- 
\accentset{\mbox{\large\bfseries .}}{q}'\in L^2([0,1);\mathbb{R}^{\mathscr{S}})$, and $r\in[0,1]$,
\begin{align}
    (1-r)\overline F_N(t,q)+r\overline F_N(t,q')-\overline F_N\left(t,(1-r)q+rq'\right)\leqslant Cr(1-r)c^{-2}| 
\accentset{\mbox{\large\bfseries .}}{q}- 
\accentset{\mbox{\large\bfseries .}}{q}'|_{L^2}^2.
    \label{e.semi_concave_q_spherical}
\end{align}
The estimate is unchanged if one adds to the Hamiltonian a Gaussian field independent of the cascade field $W_N^q$, whose law does not depend on $q$, or a deterministic affine function of $q$.
<!-- end proposition-2 -->
<!-- proof-2: body_md -->
This is~\cite[Propositions~3.7 and~3.8]{chen2025free} at fixed $t$, in the diagonal multi-species form of~\cite[Proposition~4.5]{chen2024ms}; since $t$ is fixed, the lower bound on $t$ required there for the joint semi-concavity in $(t,q)$ is not needed, and the ellipticity condition of the matrix-valued statement is void for scalar increments. The proofs use only the covariance~\eqref{e.WNq_covariance} of the cascade field, the self-overlap correction in~\eqref{e.enriched_H}, and the bound $|R_{N,s}(\sigma,\sigma')|\leqslant\lambda_{N,s}$ verified in the proof of Proposition~\ref{p.F_N_smooth}. For the last assertion, recall that the proof of~\cite[Proposition~3.7]{chen2025free} consists of H\"older's inequality applied in the amplitudes $(q^s_j-q^s_{j-1})^{1/2}$ of a finite-step path, for which the terms of the Hamiltonian that do not depend on the amplitudes play no role, and of a bound on the derivatives of the free energy in the amplitudes obtained by Gaussian integration by parts. A Gaussian field independent of the cascade field, with a law that does not depend on $q$, is such a term, and it does not affect the derivative bound; a deterministic affine function of $q$ contributes zero to the left-hand side of~\eqref{e.semi_concave_q_spherical}.
<!-- end proof-2 -->
<!-- remark-1: body_md -->
\label{r.finite_step_CS}
Let $\rho$ be a finite-step path, written as in~\eqref{e.finite_step_path}. An Abel summation gives $\mathcal K(\rho)=\sum_{i=1}^km_i(\rho_i-\rho_{i-1})$, and for $r\in[\rho_{i-1},\rho_i)$ with $i\geqslant1$ we have $\mathcal K_\rho(r)=m_i(\rho_i-r)+\sum_{j>i}m_j(\rho_j-\rho_{j-1})$, while $\mathcal K_\rho(r)=\mathcal K(\rho)$ for $r\in[0,\rho_0)$. Writing
\begin{equation}
\label{e.c_i_def}
    c_i:=b-2\sum_{j=i}^km_j(\rho_j-\rho_{j-1}),\qquad 1\leqslant i\leqslant k+1,
\end{equation}
so that $c_1=b-2\mathcal K(\rho)$, $c_{k+1}=b$, and $c_1\leqslant c_2\leqslant\cdots\leqslant c_{k+1}$, the integral in~\eqref{e.scalar_spherical_initial} can be computed explicitly:
\begin{equation}
\label{e.CS_integral_finite_step}
    \int_0^{\rho(1)}\frac{\mathrm{d} r}{b-2\mathcal K_\rho(r)}=\frac{\rho_0}{c_1}+\sum_{i=1}^k\frac{\log c_{i+1}-\log c_i}{2m_i}.
\end{equation}
<!-- end remark-1 -->
<!-- lemma-1: body_md -->
\label{l.multiplier}
Let $a\in\mathbb{R}$.
\begin{enumerate}
    \item \label{i.multiplier_existence} For every $\rho\in\mathcal Q_1$, $\ell>0$, and $r\geqslant0$,
    \begin{equation}
    \label{e.half_line_bounds}
        \ell+2(r-\overline\rho)_+\leqslant d_{\rho,\ell}(r)\leqslant\ell+2r,
        \qquad\text{hence}\qquad
        \frac1\ell\leqslant S_a(\rho,\ell)\leqslant\frac1\ell+\frac{a^2+2\overline\rho}{\ell^2}.
    \end{equation}
    The function $\ell\mapsto S_a(\rho,\ell)$ is continuous and strictly decreasing on $(0,\infty)$, and there is a unique $\ell_a(\rho)>0$ such that $S_a(\rho,\ell_a(\rho))=1$. It satisfies
    \begin{equation}
    \label{e.uniform_gap}
        1\leqslant\ell_a(\rho)\leqslant\frac{1+\sqrt{1+4a^2+8\overline\rho}}2.
    \end{equation}
    \item \label{i.multiplier_minimizer} Let $\rho\in\mathcal Q_\infty$ and $b>2\mathcal K(\rho)$, and set $\ell:=b-2\mathcal K(\rho)$. Then $d_{\rho,\ell}(r)=b-2\mathcal K_\rho(r)$ for $r\in[0,\rho(1)]$, $d_{\rho,\ell}(r)=b+2(r-\rho(1))$ for $r\geqslant\rho(1)$, and
    \begin{equation}
    \label{e.D_b_derivative_explicit}
        \partial_b\mathcal D^\circ_a(\rho,b)=\frac12\left(1-S_a\left(\rho,b-2\mathcal K(\rho)\right)\right).
    \end{equation}
    Consequently, $b\mapsto\mathcal D^\circ_a(\rho,b)$ is strictly convex on $(2\mathcal K(\rho),\infty)$, and the infimum in~\eqref{e.scalar_initial_direct_identity} is attained at the unique point
    \begin{equation}
    \label{e.b_a_def}
        b_a(\rho):=\ell_a(\rho)+2\mathcal K(\rho)\geqslant1.
    \end{equation}
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end lemma-1 -->
<!-- proof-3: body_md -->
\emph{Part~\eqref{i.multiplier_existence}.}
The upper bound on $d_{\rho,\ell}$ follows from $(r-\rho(v))_+\leqslant r$, and the lower bound from Jensen's inequality applied to the convex function $x\mapsto(r-x)_+$. Since $2\int_0^\infty(\ell+2r)^{-2}\mathrm{d} r=\ell^{-1}$ and $2\int_0^\infty(\ell+2(r-\overline\rho)_+)^{-2}\mathrm{d} r=2\overline\rho\ell^{-2}+\ell^{-1}$, the bounds on $S_a$ follow. For fixed $r$, the function $\ell\mapsto d_{\rho,\ell}(r)^{-2}$ is continuous and strictly decreasing, and it is dominated by $(\ell_0+2(r-\overline\rho)_+)^{-2}$, which is integrable on $[0,\infty)$, for $\ell\geqslant\ell_0>0$; by dominated convergence, $\ell\mapsto S_a(\rho,\ell)$ is continuous and strictly decreasing, and by~\eqref{e.half_line_bounds}, it tends to $+\infty$ as $\ell\searrow0$ and to $0$ as $\ell\to\infty$. Hence the equation $S_a(\rho,\ell)=1$ has a unique solution $\ell_a(\rho)$. The lower bound $S_a(\rho,\ell)\geqslant\ell^{-1}$ gives $\ell_a(\rho)\geqslant1$, and the upper bound gives $\ell_a(\rho)^2-\ell_a(\rho)-(a^2+2\overline\rho)\leqslant0$, which is the upper bound in~\eqref{e.uniform_gap}.

\smallskip
\noindent\emph{Part~\eqref{i.multiplier_minimizer}.}
For $r\in[0,\rho(1)]$, the definition~\eqref{e.Krho_def} gives $\mathcal K(\rho)-\mathcal K_\rho(r)=\int_0^1(\rho(u)\vee r-\rho(u))\mathrm{d} u=\int_0^1(r-\rho(u))_+\mathrm{d} u$, so that $b-2\mathcal K_\rho(r)=d_{\rho,\ell}(r)$. For $r\geqslant\rho(1)$, we have $(r-\rho(v))_+=r-\rho(v)$ for every $v$, so that $d_{\rho,\ell}(r)=\ell+2r-2\overline\rho=b+2(r-\rho(1))$. Differentiating~\eqref{e.scalar_spherical_initial} in $b$ under the integral sign, we get
\begin{align*}
    \partial_b\mathcal D^\circ_a(\rho,b) & =-\frac{a^2}{2\ell^2}-\int_0^{\rho(1)}\frac{\mathrm{d} r}{d_{\rho,\ell}(r)^2}+\frac12\left(1-\frac1b\right),
    \\
    \frac1b & =2\int_{\rho(1)}^\infty\frac{\mathrm{d} r}{(b+2(r-\rho(1)))^2}=2\int_{\rho(1)}^\infty\frac{\mathrm{d} r}{d_{\rho,\ell}(r)^2},
\end{align*}
which is~\eqref{e.D_b_derivative_explicit}. Since $\ell\mapsto S_a(\rho,\ell)$ is strictly decreasing, $\partial_b\mathcal D^\circ_a(\rho,b)$ is strictly increasing in $b$, negative for $b<b_a(\rho)$ and positive for $b>b_a(\rho)$; this proves the strict convexity and identifies the minimizer. The bound $b_a(\rho)\geqslant1$ follows from~\eqref{e.uniform_gap} and $\mathcal K(\rho)\geqslant0$.
<!-- end proof-3 -->
<!-- lemma-2: body_md -->
\label{l.multiplier_regularity}
Let $a\in\mathbb{R}$.
\begin{enumerate}
    \item \label{i.multiplier_lipschitz} For every $\rho,\rho'\in\mathcal Q_1$,
    \begin{equation}
    \label{e.ell_lipschitz}
        |\ell_a(\rho)-\ell_a(\rho')|\leqslant2|\rho-\rho'|_{L^1},
    \end{equation}
    and, if $\rho,\rho'\in\mathcal Q_\infty$, then $|b_a(\rho)-b_a(\rho')|\leqslant4|\rho-\rho'|_{L^1}+2|\rho(1)-\rho'(1)|$.
    \item \label{i.multiplier_gradient} For $\rho\in\mathcal Q_1$, define
    \begin{equation}
    \label{e.zeta_explicit}
        \zeta_{a,\rho}(u):=1-2\int_{\rho(u)}^\infty\frac{\mathrm{d} r}{d_{\rho,\ell_a(\rho)}(r)^2},
        \qquad u\in[0,1).
    \end{equation}
    We have $\zeta_{a,\rho}\in\mathcal Q_{\infty,\leqslant1}$, and $\zeta_{a,\rho}\geqslant a^2/\ell_a(\rho)^2$. If $\rho\in\mathcal Q_\infty$, then
    \begin{equation}
    \label{e.zeta_bounded_formula}
        \zeta_{a,\rho}(u)=\frac{a^2}{\ell_a(\rho)^2}+2\int_0^{\rho(u)}\frac{\mathrm{d} r}{(b_a(\rho)-2\mathcal K_\rho(r))^2}
        \qquad\text{and}\qquad
        \zeta_{a,\rho}(1)=1-\frac1{b_a(\rho)}.
    \end{equation}
    Moreover, for every $\rho,\rho'\in\mathcal Q_1$ and $u\in[0,1)$,
    \begin{equation}
    \label{e.zeta_pointwise_stability}
        |\zeta_{a,\rho}(u)-\zeta_{a,\rho'}(u)|\leqslant2|\rho(u)-\rho'(u)|+8|\rho-\rho'|_{L^1},
    \end{equation}
    and therefore, for every $r\in[1,\infty]$ and $\rho,\rho'\in\mathcal Q_r$,
    \begin{equation}
    \label{e.scalar_gradient_lipschitz}
        |\zeta_{a,\rho}-\zeta_{a,\rho'}|_{L^r}\leqslant10|\rho-\rho'|_{L^r}.
    \end{equation}
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end lemma-2 -->
<!-- proof-4: body_md -->
\emph{Part~\eqref{i.multiplier_lipschitz}.}
Set $\delta:=|\rho-\rho'|_{L^1}$. Since the positive part is $1$-Lipschitz, $|d_{\rho,\ell}(r)-d_{\rho',\ell}(r)|\leqslant2\delta$ for every $r$ and $\ell$, so that $d_{\rho',\ell+2\delta}\geqslant d_{\rho,\ell}$ and $S_a(\rho',\ell+2\delta)\leqslant S_a(\rho,\ell)$. At $\ell=\ell_a(\rho)$, this gives $S_a(\rho',\ell_a(\rho)+2\delta)\leqslant1=S_a(\rho',\ell_a(\rho'))$, hence $\ell_a(\rho')\leqslant\ell_a(\rho)+2\delta$ by strict monotonicity. Exchanging the roles of $\rho$ and $\rho'$ proves~\eqref{e.ell_lipschitz}, and the bound on $b_a$ follows from $|\mathcal K(\rho)-\mathcal K(\rho')|\leqslant|\rho(1)-\rho'(1)|+\delta$.

\smallskip
\noindent\emph{Part~\eqref{i.multiplier_gradient}.}
Write $\ell:=\ell_a(\rho)$ and $d:=d_{\rho,\ell}$. Since $\rho$ is nondecreasing and right-continuous, and since $d^{-2}$ is positive and continuous, the path $\zeta_{a,\rho}$ is nondecreasing and right-continuous, and it is at most $1$. By the equation $S_a(\rho,\ell)=1$, we have $\zeta_{a,\rho}(u)\geqslant1-2\int_0^\infty d^{-2}=a^2/\ell^2\geqslant0$, so that $\zeta_{a,\rho}\in\mathcal Q_{\infty,\leqslant1}$. If $\rho$ is bounded, then $1-2\int_{\rho(u)}^\infty d^{-2}=a^2/\ell^2+2\int_0^{\rho(u)}d^{-2}$, which is the first formula in~\eqref{e.zeta_bounded_formula} by Lemma~\ref{l.multiplier}, part~\eqref{i.multiplier_minimizer}; and letting $u\nearrow1$ and using the same part again gives $\zeta_{a,\rho}(1)=1-2\int_{\rho(1)}^\infty d^{-2}=1-1/b_a(\rho)$.

Let now $\rho'\in\mathcal Q_1$, $\delta:=|\rho-\rho'|_{L^1}$, and $\widetilde d:=d_{\rho',\ell_a(\rho')}$. By~\eqref{e.uniform_gap}, $d\geqslant1$ and $\widetilde d\geqslant1$; by~\eqref{e.ell_lipschitz} and the $1$-Lipschitz continuity of the positive part, $\|d-\widetilde d\|_{L^\infty}\leqslant4\delta$; and by the equation $S_a=1$, we have $2\int_0^\infty d^{-2}\leqslant1$ and $2\int_0^\infty\widetilde d^{-2}\leqslant1$. For $x,y\geqslant1$,
\begin{equation*}
    |x^{-2}-y^{-2}|=|x-y|\,\frac{x+y}{x^2y^2}\leqslant|x-y|\left(x^{-2}+y^{-2}\right),
\end{equation*}
so that $\int_0^\infty|d^{-2}-\widetilde d^{-2}|\mathrm{d} r\leqslant4\delta$. Writing
\begin{equation*}
    \zeta_{a,\rho}(u)-\zeta_{a,\rho'}(u)=2\int_{\rho'(u)}^\infty\left(\widetilde d(r)^{-2}-d(r)^{-2}\right)\mathrm{d} r-2\int_{\rho(u)}^{\rho'(u)}d(r)^{-2}\mathrm{d} r
\end{equation*}
and using $d^{-2}\leqslant1$ gives~\eqref{e.zeta_pointwise_stability}. Taking the $L^r$ norm and using $\delta\leqslant|\rho-\rho'|_{L^r}$ gives~\eqref{e.scalar_gradient_lipschitz}.
<!-- end proof-4 -->
<!-- lemma-3: body_md -->
\label{l.linear_cascade_identity}
Let $c\in\mathcal Q_\infty$, and let $\mathsf W$ be a centered Gaussian field on $\mathfrak U$ with covariance $\mathbb{E}\mathsf W(\alpha)\mathsf W(\alpha')=c(\alpha\wedge\alpha')$. We have
\begin{equation}
    \mathbb{E}\log\int\exp\left(\mathsf W(\alpha)\right)\mathfrak{R}(\mathrm{d}\alpha)=\frac12\mathcal K(c)=\frac12\left(c(1)-\int_0^1c(r)\mathrm{d} r\right).
    \label{e.cascade_gaussian_identity}
\end{equation}
<!-- end lemma-3 -->
<!-- proof-5: body_md -->
For $v\in[0,1]$, set $G(v):=\mathbb{E}\log\int\exp(\sqrt v\,\mathsf W(\alpha))\mathfrak{R}(\mathrm{d}\alpha)$, which satisfies $0\leqslant G(v)\leqslant vc(1)/2$ by Jensen's inequality. The field $\sqrt v\mathsf W$ has covariance $vc(\alpha\wedge\alpha')$, which is affine in $v$. By Gaussian integration by parts in the form of~\cite[Theorem~4.6]{HJbook}, and by the invariance~\eqref{e.invariance_cascade} of the overlap law under the Lipschitz tilt $x\mapsto\sqrt vx$,
\begin{equation*}
    G'(v)=\frac12\,\mathbb{E}\left\langle c(\alpha\wedge\alpha)-c(\alpha\wedge\alpha')\right\rangle_{\mathfrak{R}^{\sqrt v\mathsf W}}=\frac12\left(c(1)-\int_0^1c(r)\mathrm{d} r\right),
\end{equation*}
which does not depend on $v$. Integrating over $[0,1]$ and using $G(0)=0$ gives~\eqref{e.cascade_gaussian_identity}. For a finite-step path $c$, the identity can also be read off from the recursion~\eqref{e.tilted_recursion} of Appendix~\ref{s.app_cascade}, the tilt being affine in the marks at every level.
<!-- end proof-5 -->
<!-- lemma-4: body_md -->
\label{l.scalar_initial_continuous_derivative}
Let $\rho\in\mathcal Q_\infty$ and $a\in\mathbb{R}$.
\begin{enumerate}
    \item \label{i.block_admissible} If $b>2\mathcal K(\rho)$, then $Z^\circ_{a,b}(\rho)$ is almost surely finite, $\log Z^\circ_{a,b}(\rho)$ is integrable, and~\eqref{e.block_representation} holds, that is, $\mathbb{E}\log Z^\circ_{a,b}(\rho)=\mathcal X_a(\rho,b)$.
    \item \label{i.block_nonadmissible} If $b\leqslant2\mathcal K(\rho)$, then $\mathbb{E}\log Z^\circ_{a,b}(\rho)=+\infty$.
    \item \label{i.block_convex} The function $b\mapsto\mathbb{E}\log Z^\circ_{a,b}(\rho)$ is convex and differentiable on $(2\mathcal K(\rho),\infty)$, with $\mathbb{E}\left\langle\tau^2\right\rangle^\circ_{\rho,b}<\infty$ and
    \begin{equation}
    \label{e.block_b_derivative}
        \partial_b\mathcal D_a^\circ(\rho,b)=\frac12-\frac12\mathbb{E}\left\langle\tau^2\right\rangle^\circ_{\rho,b}.
    \end{equation}
    Consequently, the minimizer $b_a(\rho)$ of Lemma~\ref{l.multiplier} is the unique admissible $b$ such that
    \begin{equation}
    \label{e.scalar_initial_normalization}
        \mathbb{E}\left\langle\tau^2\right\rangle^\circ_{\rho,b}=1.
    \end{equation}
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end lemma-4 -->
<!-- proof-6: body_md -->
\emph{Step 1: Finite-step paths.}\par
Let $\rho$ be as in~\eqref{e.finite_step_path}, and let $b>2\mathcal K(\rho)$. By~\eqref{e.Zcirc_tau_integrated} and~\eqref{e.equiv_cascade_fe}, applied to the nonnegative function $g(x):=x^2/(2b)$ as explained after~\eqref{e.equiv_cascade_overlaps},
\begin{equation}
\label{e.block_discrete}
    \mathbb{E}\log Z^\circ_{a,b}(\rho)=\mathbb{E}\log\sum_{\alpha\in\mathbb{N}^k}v_\alpha\exp\left(g(\sqrt2\mathsf w^\rho(\alpha)+a)\right)-\frac12\log b,
\end{equation}
as an identity in $(-\infty,+\infty]$. We compute the right-hand side with the recursive formula for averages along Poisson--Dirichlet cascades of~\cite[Theorem~2.9]{pan} or \cite[Theorem~5.25]{HJbook}, as in~\cite[Section~3]{tal.sph}. Writing $\Delta_j:=2(\rho_j-\rho_{j-1})$ and letting $z$ be a standard Gaussian random variable, define $Y_k:=g$ and, for $j$ from $k$ down to $1$,
\begin{equation}
\label{e.scalar_recursion}
    Y_{j-1}(x):=\frac1{m_j}\log\mathbb{E}\exp\left(m_jY_j\left(x+\Delta_j^{1/2}z\right)\right),
    \qquad Y_{-1}:=\mathbb{E} Y_0\left(a+\Delta_0^{1/2}z\right).
\end{equation}
The theorem is stated in~\cite{HJbook} under the assumption that $\mathbb{E}\exp(m_kg(\sqrt2\mathsf w^\rho(\alpha)+a))<\infty$, which may fail for the quadratic function $g$ even when $b$ is admissible, and we apply it to the bounded functions $g\wedge L$ instead. As $L\to\infty$, the left-hand side of the resulting identity increases to $\mathbb{E}\log\sum_\alpha v_\alpha\exp(g(\sqrt2\mathsf w^\rho(\alpha)+a))$, by monotone convergence, since $g\wedge L\geqslant0$; and at each level, the function obtained from $g\wedge L$ through~\eqref{e.scalar_recursion} increases to the function obtained from $g$, by monotone convergence in each expectation, the recursion being understood with values in $(-\infty,+\infty]$. Hence $\mathbb{E}\log\sum_\alpha v_\alpha\exp(g(\sqrt2\mathsf w^\rho(\alpha)+a))=Y_{-1}$ in $(-\infty,+\infty]$, and it remains to compute the recursion. If $Y_j(x)=x^2/(2c_{j+1})+d_{j+1}$ for some $c_{j+1}>m_j\Delta_j$ and $d_{j+1}\in\mathbb{R}$, then a Gaussian computation gives $Y_{j-1}(x)=x^2/(2c_j)+d_j$ with
\begin{equation*}
    c_j=c_{j+1}-m_j\Delta_j,
    \qquad
    d_j=d_{j+1}+\frac1{2m_j}\left(\log c_{j+1}-\log c_j\right),
\end{equation*}
while $Y_{j-1}\equiv+\infty$ if $c_{j+1}\leqslant m_j\Delta_j$. Starting from $c_{k+1}=b$ and $d_{k+1}=0$, the constants $c_j$ are those of~\eqref{e.c_i_def}, and since they are nondecreasing in $j$, they are all positive if and only if $c_1=b-2\mathcal K(\rho)>0$. 
                                                                                                                                                                    
Finally, $Y_{-1}=(a^2+\Delta_0)/(2c_1)+d_1$, and comparing with~\eqref{e.CS_integral_finite_step} gives
\begin{equation}
\label{e.X0_explicit}
    Y_{-1}=\frac{a^2}{2(b-2\mathcal K(\rho))}+\int_0^{\rho(1)}\frac{\mathrm{d} r}{b-2\mathcal K_\rho(r)}.
\end{equation}
Together with~\eqref{e.block_discrete}, this proves $\mathbb{E}\log Z^\circ_{a,b}(\rho)=\mathcal X_a(\rho,b)$ for finite-step paths. In particular, $\mathbb{E}\log Z^\circ_{a,b}(\rho)<\infty$, so that $Z^\circ_{a,b}(\rho)$ is almost surely finite; and $\log Z^\circ_{a,b}(\rho)$ is bounded from below by a deterministic constant, as we now check for general paths, so that it is integrable.

\smallskip
\noindent\emph{Step 2: Cutoff and a deterministic lower bound.}\par
Let $\rho\in\mathcal Q_\infty$ and $b\in\mathbb{R}$. For $L>0$, let $Z^\circ_{a,b,L}(\rho)$ and $\left\langle\cdot\right\rangle^\circ_{\rho,b,L}$ be defined as $Z^\circ_{a,b}(\rho)$ and $\left\langle\cdot\right\rangle^\circ_{\rho,b}$ in~\eqref{e.scalar_direct_initial_functional}, with the integration in $\tau$ restricted to $[-L,L]$, and let $\gamma_L$ be the normalized restriction of $\gamma$ to $[-L,L]$. By Jensen's inequality under $\gamma_L\otimes\mathfrak{R}$, and since $\int\tau\gamma_L(\mathrm{d}\tau)=0$,
\begin{equation}
\label{e.block_deterministic_lower_bound}
    \log Z^\circ_{a,b,L}(\rho)\geqslant\log\gamma([-L,L])-\frac{|b-1|}2L^2=:-C_{b,L}.
\end{equation}
Since $Z^\circ_{a,b,L}(\rho)$ increases to $Z^\circ_{a,b}(\rho)$ as $L\to\infty$, and since $\log Z^\circ_{a,b,L}(\rho)\geqslant-C_{b,1}$ for $L\geqslant1$, the expectation $\mathbb{E}\log Z^\circ_{a,b}(\rho)$ is well defined in $(-\infty,+\infty]$, and $\mathbb{E}\log Z^\circ_{a,b,L}(\rho)\to\mathbb{E}\log Z^\circ_{a,b}(\rho)$ as $L\to\infty$, by monotone convergence; this holds for every $b\in\mathbb{R}$.

\smallskip
\noindent\emph{Step 3: Admissible $b$ for general paths.}\par
Let $\rho\in\mathcal Q_\infty$ and $b>2\mathcal K(\rho)$. For $\delta>0$, we discretize $\rho$ by setting
\begin{equation*}
    \rho^{(\delta)}:=\min\left\{\rho(1),\ \delta\left(\left\lfloor\rho/\delta\right\rfloor+1\right)\right\}.
\end{equation*}
The path $\rho^{(\delta)}$ is a finite-step path, since $\rho$ is bounded, nondecreasing, and right-continuous, and it satisfies $\rho\leqslant\rho^{(\delta)}\leqslant\rho+\delta$ and $\rho^{(\delta)}(1)=\rho(1)$. Since $\rho^{(\delta)}\geqslant\rho$ with the same endpoint, $\mathcal K(\rho^{(\delta)})\leqslant\mathcal K(\rho)$, so that every $b'>2\mathcal K(\rho)$ is admissible for $\rho^{(\delta)}$. We compare the block at $(\rho,b)$ with the blocks at $(\rho^{(\delta)},b\pm2\delta)$, which Step~1 computes, along an interpolation in which the path and the multiplier vary simultaneously, the multiplier absorbing the effect of the change of path.

For $L>0$ and $b'\in\mathbb{R}$, the function $g_{L,b'}(x):=\log\int_{-L}^L\exp(x\tau-\frac{b'}2\tau^2)\frac{\mathrm{d}\tau}{\sqrt{2\pi}}$ is smooth, with $|g_{L,b'}'|\leqslant L$, and $Z^\circ_{a,b',L}(\rho)=\int\exp(g_{L,b'}(\sqrt2w^\rho(\alpha)+a))\mathfrak{R}(\mathrm{d}\alpha)$. Set $\kappa:=\rho^{(\delta)}-\rho$, so that $0\leqslant\kappa\leqslant\delta$ and $\kappa(1)=0$, and, for $s\in[0,1]$ and $\beta\in\mathbb{R}$, let $\rho_s:=\rho+s\kappa$ and $b_s:=b+s\beta$; we realize the fields jointly as $w^{\rho_s}=\sqrt{1-s}\,w^\rho+\sqrt s\,w^{\rho^{(\delta)}}$, with $w^\rho$ and $w^{\rho^{(\delta)}}$ independent. Gaussian integration by parts and the invariance~\eqref{e.invariance_cascade}, as in the proof of~\cite[Proposition~5.1]{chen2025free}, together with the fact that the derivative of $\log Z^\circ_{a,b',L}(\rho)$ in $b'$ is $-\frac12\left\langle\tau^2\right\rangle^\circ_{\rho,b',L}$, give
\begin{equation}
\label{e.cutoff_IBP}
    \frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d} s}\mathbb{E}\log Z^\circ_{a,b_s,L}(\rho_s)=-\mathbb{E}\left\langle\kappa(\alpha\wedge\alpha')\tau\tau'\right\rangle^\circ_{\rho_s,b_s,L}-\frac\beta2\,\mathbb{E}\left\langle\tau^2\right\rangle^\circ_{\rho_s,b_s,L},
\end{equation}
where the diagonal term of the integration by parts vanishes because $\kappa(1)=0$, and where we used that $g_{L,b_s}'(\sqrt2w^{\rho_s}(\alpha)+a)$ is the conditional mean of $\tau$ given $\alpha$ under $\left\langle\cdot\right\rangle^\circ_{\rho_s,b_s,L}$. Since $0\leqslant\kappa\leqslant\delta$ and $|\tau\tau'|\leqslant\frac12(\tau^2+\tau'^2)$, the first term on the right-hand side of~\eqref{e.cutoff_IBP} is at most $\delta\,\mathbb{E}\left\langle\tau^2\right\rangle^\circ_{\rho_s,b_s,L}$ in absolute value. The derivative in~\eqref{e.cutoff_IBP} is therefore nonpositive when $\beta=2\delta$, and nonnegative when $\beta=-2\delta$. Integrating over $s\in[0,1]$ in both cases, we obtain
\begin{equation*}
    \mathbb{E}\log Z^\circ_{a,b+2\delta,L}(\rho^{(\delta)})\leqslant\mathbb{E}\log Z^\circ_{a,b,L}(\rho)\leqslant\mathbb{E}\log Z^\circ_{a,b-2\delta,L}(\rho^{(\delta)}),
\end{equation*}
and letting $L\to\infty$, by the monotone convergence noted in Step~2, gives
\begin{equation}
\label{e.block_sandwich}
    \mathbb{E}\log Z^\circ_{a,b+2\delta}(\rho^{(\delta)})\leqslant\mathbb{E}\log Z^\circ_{a,b}(\rho)\leqslant\mathbb{E}\log Z^\circ_{a,b-2\delta}(\rho^{(\delta)}).
\end{equation}
For $4\delta<b-2\mathcal K(\rho)$, the multipliers $b\pm2\delta$ are admissible for $\rho^{(\delta)}$, and Step~1 identifies the outer terms in~\eqref{e.block_sandwich} with $\mathcal X_a(\rho^{(\delta)},b\pm2\delta)$. Since $|\mathcal K_{\rho^{(\delta)}}(r)-\mathcal K_\rho(r)|\leqslant\delta$ uniformly in $r\in[0,\rho(1)]$, the denominators in~\eqref{e.X_a_def} evaluated at $(\rho^{(\delta)},b\pm2\delta)$ are bounded from below by $\frac12(b-2\mathcal K(\rho))$ once $8\delta\leqslant b-2\mathcal K(\rho)$, and dominated convergence gives $\mathcal X_a(\rho^{(\delta)},b\pm2\delta)\to\mathcal X_a(\rho,b)$ as $\delta\to0$. Letting $\delta\to0$ in~\eqref{e.block_sandwich} therefore yields $\mathbb{E}\log Z^\circ_{a,b}(\rho)=\mathcal X_a(\rho,b)<\infty$. In particular, $Z^\circ_{a,b}(\rho)$ is almost surely finite, and $\log Z^\circ_{a,b}(\rho)\geqslant-C_{b,1}$ is integrable. This completes the proof of part~\eqref{i.block_admissible}.

\smallskip
\noindent\emph{Step 4: Non-admissible $b$.}\par
Let $b\leqslant2\mathcal K(\rho)$ and $T>0$, and let $J$ be the interval $[T,2T]$ if $a\geqslant0$ and $[-2T,-T]$ otherwise, so that $a\tau\geqslant0$ on $J$. The expectation $\mathbb{E}\log Z^\circ_{a,b}(\rho)$ is well defined in $(-\infty,+\infty]$, by Step~2. Restricting the integral in $\tau$ to $J$ and applying Jensen's inequality with respect to the normalized Lebesgue measure on $J$, we obtain
\begin{align*}
    \mathbb{E}\log Z^\circ_{a,b}(\rho)
    &\geqslant\log\frac{T}{\sqrt{2\pi}}+\frac1T\int_J\left(\mathbb{E}\log\int\exp\left(\sqrt2\tau w^\rho(\alpha)\right)\mathfrak{R}(\mathrm{d}\alpha)+a\tau-\frac b2\tau^2\right)\mathrm{d}\tau\\
    &=\log\frac{T}{\sqrt{2\pi}}+\frac1T\int_J\left(\left(\mathcal K(\rho)-\frac b2\right)\tau^2+a\tau\right)\mathrm{d}\tau\geqslant\log\frac{T}{\sqrt{2\pi}},
\end{align*}
where we used Lemma~\ref{l.linear_cascade_identity} with the path $2\tau^2\rho$, for which $\mathcal K(2\tau^2\rho)=2\tau^2\mathcal K(\rho)$. Letting $T\to\infty$ proves part~\eqref{i.block_nonadmissible}.

\smallskip
\noindent\emph{Step 5: Dependence on $b$.}\par
Since $Z^\circ_{a,b'}(\rho)$ is nonincreasing in $b'$, part~\eqref{i.block_admissible}, applied along a sequence of admissible values of $b'$ decreasing to $2\mathcal K(\rho)$, shows that almost surely $Z^\circ_{a,b'}(\rho)<\infty$ for every $b'>2\mathcal K(\rho)$. On this event, the function $b'\mapsto\log Z^\circ_{a,b'}(\rho)$ is the logarithm of the Laplace transform, in the variable $b'/2$, of the image of the positive measure $\exp((\sqrt2w^\rho(\alpha)+a)\tau+\frac12\tau^2)\mathfrak{R}(\mathrm{d}\alpha)\gamma(\mathrm{d}\tau)$ under $(\tau,\alpha)\mapsto\tau^2$; it is therefore convex and differentiable on the open interval $(2\mathcal K(\rho),\infty)$, with derivative $-\frac12\left\langle\tau^2\right\rangle^\circ_{\rho,b'}$. Fix $b>2\mathcal K(\rho)$. By convexity, for $\varepsilon>0$, the difference quotients $\varepsilon^{-1}(\log Z^\circ_{a,b+\varepsilon}(\rho)-\log Z^\circ_{a,b}(\rho))$ decrease to $-\frac12\left\langle\tau^2\right\rangle^\circ_{\rho,b}$ as $\varepsilon\searrow0$, and they are bounded above by the integrable random variable obtained for $\varepsilon=1$. By monotone convergence, $-\frac12\mathbb{E}\left\langle\tau^2\right\rangle^\circ_{\rho,b}$ is the right derivative at $b$ of the convex function $b'\mapsto\mathbb{E}\log Z^\circ_{a,b'}(\rho)$, which is finite on $(2\mathcal K(\rho),\infty)$ by part~\eqref{i.block_admissible}; in particular $\mathbb{E}\left\langle\tau^2\right\rangle^\circ_{\rho,b}<\infty$. The same argument with $\varepsilon<0$ identifies the left derivative with the same quantity. Hence $b'\mapsto\mathbb{E}\log Z^\circ_{a,b'}(\rho)$ is differentiable, with derivative $-\frac12\mathbb{E}\left\langle\tau^2\right\rangle^\circ_{\rho,b'}$, and~\eqref{e.block_b_derivative} follows from~\eqref{e.block_representation}. Finally, by Lemma~\ref{l.multiplier}, part~\eqref{i.multiplier_minimizer}, the derivative $\partial_b\mathcal D^\circ_a(\rho,b)$ vanishes exactly at $b=b_a(\rho)$, which is~\eqref{e.scalar_initial_normalization}.
<!-- end proof-6 -->
<!-- proposition-3: body_md -->
\label{l.psi_spherical_smooth}
Let $a\in\mathbb{R}$.
\begin{enumerate}
    \item \label{i.psi_lipschitz} For every $\rho,\rho'\in\mathcal Q_\infty$,
    \begin{equation}
    \label{e.scalar_regular_lipschitz_continuous}
        |\psi^\circ_a(\rho)-\psi^\circ_a(\rho')|\leqslant|\rho-\rho'|_{L^1}.
    \end{equation}
    Consequently, $\psi^\circ_a$ extends uniquely by continuity to $\mathcal Q_1$, and~\eqref{e.scalar_regular_lipschitz_continuous} holds on $\mathcal Q_1$.
    \item \label{i.zeta_derivative} For every $\rho,\rho'\in\mathcal Q_2$,
    \begin{equation}
    \label{e.scalar_quadratic_remainder}
        \left|\psi^\circ_a(\rho')-\psi_a^\circ(\rho)-\int_0^1(\rho'-\rho)\,\zeta_{a,\rho}\right|\leqslant5|\rho'-\rho|_{L^2}^2.
    \end{equation}
    In particular, $\psi^\circ_a$ is Fr\'echet differentiable on $\mathcal Q_2$, relative to $\mathcal Q_2$, with derivative $\zeta_{a,\rho}$ at $\rho$.
                                                                                                                                   
                     
                                                   
                                                                                                                                  
                   
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end proposition-3 -->
<!-- proof-7: body_md -->
\emph{Step 1: The functional on the half-line.}\par
For $\rho\in\mathcal Q_\infty$ and $\ell>0$, set $\widehat J_a(\rho,\ell):=\mathcal D^\circ_a(\rho,\ell+2\mathcal K(\rho))$, so that, by Lemma~\ref{l.multiplier},
\begin{equation}
\label{e.psi_as_min}
    \psi^\circ_a(\rho)=-\inf_{\ell>0}\widehat J_a(\rho,\ell)=-\widehat J_a\left(\rho,\ell_a(\rho)\right).
\end{equation}
Let $R>\rho(1)$, and write $b:=\ell+2\mathcal K(\rho)$. By part~\eqref{i.multiplier_minimizer} of Lemma~\ref{l.multiplier}, $d_{\rho,\ell}(r)=b+2(r-\rho(1))$ for $r\geqslant\rho(1)$, so that $\int_{\rho(1)}^Rd_{\rho,\ell}(r)^{-1}\mathrm{d} r=\frac12\log d_{\rho,\ell}(R)-\frac12\log b$; since moreover $\frac12(b-1)-\rho(1)=\frac12(\ell-1)-\int_0^1\rho$, the definition~\eqref{e.scalar_spherical_initial} and the same part of Lemma~\ref{l.multiplier} give
\begin{equation}
\label{e.J_hat_half_line}
    \widehat J_a(\rho,\ell)=\frac{a^2}{2\ell}+\int_0^R\frac{\mathrm{d} r}{d_{\rho,\ell}(r)}-\frac12\log d_{\rho,\ell}(R)+\frac{\ell-1}2-\int_0^1\rho(u)\mathrm{d} u.
\end{equation}
The right-hand side does not depend on the choice of $R>\rho(1)$, and the endpoint $\rho(1)$ no longer appears in it explicitly: the path enters only through $d_{\rho,\ell}$ and through its integral.

\smallskip
\noindent\emph{Step 2: Derivative along a segment, at fixed $\ell$.}\par
Let $\rho,\rho'\in\mathcal Q_\infty$, $\kappa:=\rho'-\rho$, and $\rho_s:=\rho+s\kappa$ for $s\in[0,1]$, which belongs to $\mathcal Q_\infty$ with $\rho_s(1)=(1-s)\rho(1)+s\rho'(1)$. We fix $R>\max\{\rho(1),\rho'(1)\}$, which exceeds $\rho_s(1)$ for every $s$, and $\ell>0$, and we show that $s\mapsto\widehat J_a(\rho_s,\ell)$ is differentiable on $[0,1]$, with
\begin{equation}
\label{e.J_hat_s_derivative}
    \frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d} s}\widehat J_a(\rho_s,\ell)=-\int_0^1\kappa(u)\left(1-2\int_{\rho_s(u)}^\infty\frac{\mathrm{d} r}{d_{\rho_s,\ell}(r)^2}\right)\mathrm{d} u,
\end{equation}
and that the right-hand side of~\eqref{e.J_hat_s_derivative} is a continuous function of $(s,\ell)\in[0,1]\times(0,\infty)$. Since the positive part is $1$-Lipschitz, we have $|d_{\rho_{s'},\ell}(r)-d_{\rho_s,\ell}(r)|\leqslant2|s'-s|\,|\kappa|_{L^1}$ for every $r\geqslant0$ and $s,s'\in[0,1]$, and $d_{\rho_s,\ell}\geqslant\ell$; the difference quotients of $s\mapsto d_{\rho_s,\ell}(r)^{-1}$ are therefore bounded by $2|\kappa|_{L^1}\ell^{-2}$, uniformly in $r$. Fix $s\in[0,1]$. For every $r\geqslant0$ and every $u$ such that $\rho_s(u)\ne r$, the function $s'\mapsto(r-\rho_{s'}(u))_+$ is differentiable at $s'=s$, with derivative $-\kappa(u)\mathds{1}_{\{r>\rho_s(u)\}}$. Since the sets $\{u:\rho_s(u)=r\}$, $r\geqslant0$, are disjoint, at most countably many of them have positive measure, and for every other $r$, dominated convergence gives
\begin{equation*}
    \frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d} s}d_{\rho_s,\ell}(r)=-2\int_0^1\kappa(u)\mathds{1}_{\{r>\rho_s(u)\}}\mathrm{d} u.
\end{equation*}
By dominated convergence again, now in the variable $r\in[0,R]$, and by Fubini's theorem, using that $\rho_s(u)<R$ for every $u$,
\begin{equation*}
    \frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d} s}\int_0^R\frac{\mathrm{d} r}{d_{\rho_s,\ell}(r)}=\int_0^R\frac{2\int_0^1\kappa(u)\mathds{1}_{\{r>\rho_s(u)\}}\mathrm{d} u}{d_{\rho_s,\ell}(r)^2}\mathrm{d} r=2\int_0^1\kappa(u)\int_{\rho_s(u)}^R\frac{\mathrm{d} r}{d_{\rho_s,\ell}(r)^2}\mathrm{d} u.
\end{equation*}
For the logarithmic term, since $R\geqslant\rho_s(u)$ for every $u$, we have $d_{\rho_s,\ell}(R)=\ell+2R-2\int_0^1\rho_s$, which is affine in $s$ with derivative $-2\int_0^1\kappa$; and since $d_{\rho_s,\ell}(r)=d_{\rho_s,\ell}(R)+2(r-R)$ for $r\geqslant R$, we have $d_{\rho_s,\ell}(R)^{-1}=2\int_R^\infty d_{\rho_s,\ell}(r)^{-2}\mathrm{d} r$. Hence
\begin{equation*}
    \frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d} s}\left(-\frac12\log d_{\rho_s,\ell}(R)\right)=\frac{\int_0^1\kappa}{d_{\rho_s,\ell}(R)}=2\int_0^1\kappa(u)\int_R^\infty\frac{\mathrm{d} r}{d_{\rho_s,\ell}(r)^2}\mathrm{d} u.
\end{equation*}
Adding these two contributions to the derivative $-\int_0^1\kappa$ of the last term in~\eqref{e.J_hat_half_line} gives~\eqref{e.J_hat_s_derivative}. For the joint continuity, let $(s',\ell')\to(s,\ell)$. Then $\rho_{s'}(u)\to\rho_s(u)$ for every $u$, and $d_{\rho_{s'},\ell'}\to d_{\rho_s,\ell}$ uniformly on $[0,\infty)$, while, by~\eqref{e.half_line_bounds}, for $\ell'\geqslant\ell/2$ the functions $d_{\rho_{s'},\ell'}^{-2}$ are bounded by $(\ell/2+2(r-\overline\rho\vee\overline\rho')_+)^{-2}$, which is integrable on $[0,\infty)$. By dominated convergence, the inner integrals in~\eqref{e.J_hat_s_derivative} converge for every $u$, and they are bounded uniformly in $u$; since $\kappa$ is bounded, the right-hand side of~\eqref{e.J_hat_s_derivative} converges as well.

\smallskip
\noindent\emph{Step 3: The envelope argument.}\par
With the notation of Step~2, set $\ell_s:=\ell_a(\rho_s)$ and $V(s):=\widehat J_a(\rho_s,\ell_s)=\inf_{\ell>0}\widehat J_a(\rho_s,\ell)$, so that $\psi^\circ_a(\rho_s)=-V(s)$ by~\eqref{e.psi_as_min}. By~\eqref{e.ell_lipschitz}, $|\ell_{s'}-\ell_s|\leqslant2|s'-s|\,|\kappa|_{L^1}$, so $s\mapsto\ell_s$ is continuous, and $\ell_s\geqslant1$ by~\eqref{e.uniform_gap}. For $s,s'\in[0,1]$, the minimality of $\ell_s$ and of $\ell_{s'}$ gives
\begin{equation}
\label{e.envelope_sandwich}
    \widehat J_a(\rho_{s'},\ell_{s'})-\widehat J_a(\rho_s,\ell_{s'})\leqslant V(s')-V(s)\leqslant\widehat J_a(\rho_{s'},\ell_s)-\widehat J_a(\rho_s,\ell_s).
\end{equation}
By Step~2 and the mean value theorem, the left-hand side of~\eqref{e.envelope_sandwich} is $(s'-s)$ times the right-hand side of~\eqref{e.J_hat_s_derivative} evaluated at $\ell=\ell_{s'}$ and at some point between $s$ and $s'$, and similarly for the right-hand side of~\eqref{e.envelope_sandwich}, with $\ell=\ell_s$. Dividing by $s'-s$ and letting $s'\to s$, the continuity of $s\mapsto\ell_s$ and the joint continuity established in Step~2 show that both bounds converge to the right-hand side of~\eqref{e.J_hat_s_derivative} at $\ell=\ell_s$, which is $-\int_0^1\kappa\,\zeta_{a,\rho_s}$ by~\eqref{e.zeta_explicit}. Hence $V$ is differentiable on $[0,1]$, and
\begin{equation}
\label{e.segment_derivative}
    \frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d} s}\psi^\circ_a(\rho_s)=\int_0^1\kappa(u)\zeta_{a,\rho_s}(u)\mathrm{d} u.
\end{equation}
This is the envelope theorem: the minimizer does not need to be differentiated. By~\eqref{e.scalar_gradient_lipschitz} with $r=1$, the right-hand side of~\eqref{e.segment_derivative} is a continuous function of $s$, so that~\eqref{e.segment_derivative} can be integrated over $[0,1]$.

\smallskip
\noindent\emph{Step 4: Conclusion.}\par
Since $0\leqslant\zeta_{a,\rho_s}\leqslant1$, integrating~\eqref{e.segment_derivative} gives $|\psi^\circ_a(\rho')-\psi^\circ_a(\rho)|\leqslant|\kappa|_{L^1}$, which is~\eqref{e.scalar_regular_lipschitz_continuous} on $\mathcal Q_\infty$; and by~\eqref{e.scalar_gradient_lipschitz} with $r=2$,
\begin{multline*}
    \left|\psi^\circ_a(\rho')-\psi^\circ_a(\rho)-\int_0^1\kappa\,\zeta_{a,\rho}\right|=\left|\int_0^1\int_0^1\kappa(u)\left(\zeta_{a,\rho_s}(u)-\zeta_{a,\rho}(u)\right)\mathrm{d} u\,\mathrm{d} s\right|
    \\
    \leqslant\int_0^1|\kappa|_{L^2}\,10s|\kappa|_{L^2}\mathrm{d} s=5|\kappa|_{L^2}^2,
\end{multline*}
which is~\eqref{e.scalar_quadratic_remainder} on $\mathcal Q_\infty$. Since $\mathcal Q_\infty$ is dense in $\mathcal Q_1$ for the $L^1$ norm, \eqref{e.scalar_regular_lipschitz_continuous} shows that $\psi^\circ_a$ extends uniquely by continuity to $\mathcal Q_1$, and the extension satisfies the same estimate. For $\rho,\rho'\in\mathcal Q_2$, the truncations $\rho\wedge m$ and $\rho'\wedge m$ belong to $\mathcal Q_\infty$ and converge to $\rho$ and $\rho'$ in $L^1$ and in $L^2$ as $m\to\infty$, so that $\psi^\circ_a(\rho\wedge m)\to\psi^\circ_a(\rho)$, and $\zeta_{a,\rho\wedge m}\to\zeta_{a,\rho}$ in $L^2$ by~\eqref{e.scalar_gradient_lipschitz}; passing to the limit in~\eqref{e.scalar_quadratic_remainder} proves it on $\mathcal Q_2$. Finally, \eqref{e.scalar_quadratic_remainder} says that the remainder is $O(|\rho'-\rho|_{L^2}^2)$ as $\rho'\to\rho$ in $\mathcal Q_2$, which implies the Fr\'echet differentiability relative to $\mathcal Q_2$.
<!-- end proof-7 -->
<!-- lemma-5: body_md -->
\label{l.psi_convex}
For every $q_0,q_1\in\mathcal Q_1^{\mathscr{S}}$ and every $c\in[0,1]$, we have $\psi\left((1-c)q_0+cq_1\right)\leqslant (1-c)\psi(q_0)+c\psi(q_1)$. The same holds for $\psi_\lambda$, for every probability vector $\lambda$ with positive entries.
<!-- end lemma-5 -->
<!-- proof-8: body_md -->
Since $\psi_\lambda$ is a positive linear combination of the functions $\psi^\circ_{h^s}$, it suffices to prove that $\psi_a^\circ$ is convex on $\mathcal Q_1$, for every $a\in\mathbb{R}$. By the Lipschitz continuity~\eqref{e.scalar_regular_lipschitz_continuous} and the density of finite-step paths, it suffices to prove the convexity inequality for two finite-step paths on a common partition $0=m_0<m_1<\cdots<m_k<m_{k+1}=1$. Along the segment between two such paths, the partition stays fixed and the values $\rho_0\leqslant\cdots\leqslant\rho_k$ move affinely; we parametrize them by the increments $t_i:=\rho_i-\rho_{i-1}\geqslant0$, $0\leqslant i\leqslant k$, which depend affinely on the path. It is therefore enough to prove that $\psi^\circ_a(\rho)$ is a convex function of $t=(t_0,\ldots,t_k)\in\mathbb{R}_+^{k+1}$.

We use the explicit form of $\mathcal D^\circ_a$ given in Remark~\ref{r.finite_step_CS}, and the variable $\ell=b-2\mathcal K(\rho)=c_1$ of Lemma~\ref{l.multiplier}, which ranges over $(0,\infty)$. In terms of $\ell$ and $t$, we have $c_{i+1}=\ell+2\sum_{j=1}^im_jt_j$ for $0\leqslant i\leqslant k$, $\rho_0=t_0$, $\rho_k=\sum_{i=0}^kt_i$, and, by~\eqref{e.CS_integral_finite_step},
\begin{equation*}
    \mathcal D^\circ_a(\rho,b)=\frac{a^2}{2\ell}+\frac{t_0}{\ell}+\sum_{i=1}^k\frac{\log c_{i+1}-\log c_i}{2m_i}+\frac12\left(c_{k+1}-1-\log c_{k+1}\right)-\sum_{i=0}^kt_i=:J_{\ell}(t).
\end{equation*}
When $k=0$, that is, when $\rho$ is constant, there is no logarithmic term and $J_{\ell}$ is an affine function of $t_0$. For $k\geqslant1$ and fixed $\ell$, we collect the logarithmic terms: since $c_1=\ell$ does not depend on $t$,
\begin{equation*}
    J_{\ell}(t)=\sum_{j=2}^k\left(\frac1{2m_{j-1}}-\frac1{2m_j}\right)\log c_j+\left(\frac1{2m_k}-\frac12\right)\log c_{k+1}+\text{(affine function of $t$)}.
\end{equation*}
The coefficients in front of the logarithms are nonnegative since $m_1<\cdots<m_k<1$, and each $c_j$ is a positive affine function of $t$. Hence, in all cases, $J_{\ell}$ is concave in $t$, and $\psi_a^\circ(\rho)=\sup_{\ell>0}(-J_{\ell}(t))$ is a supremum of convex functions of $t$, hence convex.
<!-- end proof-8 -->
<!-- corollary-1: body_md -->
\label{c.psi_multi_species}
Let $\lambda,\lambda'$ be probability vectors with positive entries. For every $\pi,\pi'\in\mathcal Q_1^{\mathscr{S}}$,
\begin{equation}
\label{e.psi_lambda_lipschitz}
    |\psi_\lambda(\pi)-\psi_\lambda(\pi')|\leqslant|\pi-\pi'|_{L^1}
\end{equation}
and
\begin{equation}
\label{e.derivative_stability}
    |\partial_q\psi_{\lambda'}(\pi')-\partial_q\psi_\lambda(\pi)|_{L^1}\leqslant\sum_{s\in\mathscr{S}}|\lambda'_s-\lambda_s|+10|\pi'-\pi|_{L^1}.
\end{equation}
For every $\pi,\pi'\in\mathcal Q_2^{\mathscr{S}}$,
\begin{equation}
\label{e.psi_quadratic_remainder}
    \left|\psi_\lambda(\pi')-\psi_\lambda(\pi)-\left\langle\pi'-\pi,\partial_q\psi_\lambda(\pi)\right\rangle_{L^2}\right|\leqslant5|\pi'-\pi|_{L^2}^2.
\end{equation}
<!-- end corollary-1 -->
<!-- proof-9: body_md -->
Since $\mathbb{R}^{\mathscr{S}}$ carries the Euclidean norm, we have $\sum_s\lambda_s|x_s|\leqslant|x|$ and $|x|\leqslant\sum_s|x_s|$ for $x\in\mathbb{R}^{\mathscr{S}}$. The bound~\eqref{e.psi_lambda_lipschitz} follows from~\eqref{e.scalar_regular_lipschitz_continuous}, since $|\psi_\lambda(\pi)-\psi_\lambda(\pi')|\leqslant\sum_s\lambda_s|\pi^s-\pi'^s|_{L^1}\leqslant|\pi-\pi'|_{L^1}$. For~\eqref{e.derivative_stability}, we write $\lambda'_s\zeta_{h^s,\pi'^s}-\lambda_s\zeta_{h^s,\pi^s}=(\lambda'_s-\lambda_s)\zeta_{h^s,\pi'^s}+\lambda_s(\zeta_{h^s,\pi'^s}-\zeta_{h^s,\pi^s})$, use $0\leqslant\zeta\leqslant1$ and~\eqref{e.scalar_gradient_lipschitz}, and sum over $s$. The remainder estimate~\eqref{e.psi_quadratic_remainder} follows from~\eqref{e.scalar_quadratic_remainder} applied to each species, since $\sum_s\lambda_s|\pi'^s-\pi^s|_{L^2}^2\leqslant|\pi'-\pi|_{L^2}^2$.
<!-- end proof-9 -->
<!-- proposition-4: body_md -->
\label{l.initial_condition}
For every $q\in\mathcal Q_1^{\mathscr{S}}$, we have
\begin{equation}
    \lim_{N\to\infty}\overline F_N(0,q)=\psi(q).
    \label{e.initial_condition_limit}
\end{equation}
<!-- end proposition-4 -->
<!-- proof-10: body_md -->
Since $\overline F_N(0,\cdot)$ and $\psi$ are both $1$-Lipschitz for the $L^1$ norm, by~\eqref{e.F_N_Lipschitz} and~\eqref{e.psi_lambda_lipschitz}, and since finite-step paths are dense in $\mathcal Q_1^{\mathscr{S}}$, it suffices to prove~\eqref{e.initial_condition_limit} when every $q^s$ is a finite-step path, which we assume from now on.

\smallskip
\noindent\emph{Step 1: Reduction to one species.}\par
Since $P_N$ is a product measure over the species, and since the field $\sqrt2W_N^q+\sum_sh^s\sum_{i\in I_{N,s}}\sigma_i$ is linear in $\sigma$, we have, for every $\alpha$,
\begin{equation*}
    \int\exp\left(\sqrt2W^q_N(\sigma,\alpha)+\sum_{s\in\mathscr{S}}h^s\sum_{i\in I_{N,s}}\sigma_i\right)P_N(\mathrm{d}\sigma)=\prod_{s\in\mathscr{S}}\Lambda_{N_s}\left(\sqrt2\,w^{q^s}_{I_{N,s}}(\alpha)+h^s\vec{\mathbf{1}}\right),
\end{equation*}
where $N_s:=|I_{N,s}|$ and $w^{q^s}_{I_{N,s}}:=(w_i^{q^s})_{i\in I_{N,s}}$. The logarithm of the right-hand side is a Lipschitz function of the Gaussian fields, since $|\nabla\log\Lambda_n|\leqslant\sqrt n$. By~\eqref{e.equiv_cascade_fe}, applied with a common partition for the paths $q^s$, the expectation of the logarithm of its integral against $\mathfrak{R}$ can be computed with the discrete cascade; the tilt is then a sum over the species of functions of the marks of the coordinates of that species, and by the additivity of the recursive formula over independent groups of marks, Lemma~\ref{l.tilted_cascade}, part~\eqref{i.tilted_additivity}, it equals the sum over $s$ of the corresponding quantities for a single species, that is,
\begin{equation}
\label{e.initial_species_decomposition}
    \overline F_N(0,q)=\sum_{s\in\mathscr{S}}\lambda_{N,s}\,\overline F^\circ_{N_s,h^s}(q^s).
\end{equation}
Since $\lambda_{N,s}\to\lambda_{\infty,s}$, it suffices to prove that, for every finite-step $\rho\in\mathcal Q_\infty$ and $a\in\mathbb{R}$, we have
\begin{equation}
\label{e.one_species_limit}
    \lim_{n\to\infty}\overline F^\circ_{n,a}(\rho)=\psi^\circ_a(\rho).
\end{equation}

\smallskip
\noindent\emph{Step 2: The Gaussian model.}\par
Let $\rho$ be a finite-step path, written as in~\eqref{e.finite_step_path}, and let $b>2\mathcal K(\rho)$. We use the discrete cascade with $n$ marks per node, and we let $\mathsf v_i(\alpha):=\sqrt2\mathsf w^\rho_i(\alpha)+a$, $1\leqslant i\leqslant n$, where the $\mathsf w^\rho_i$ are the discrete fields~\eqref{e.discrete_field} built from the marks of coordinate $i$. We write $\mathsf v(\alpha):=(\mathsf v_i(\alpha))_{i\leqslant n}$, so that, by~\eqref{e.equiv_cascade_fe}, $\overline F^\circ_{n,a}(\rho)=-\frac1n\mathbb{E}\log A_n+\rho(1)$ with $A_n:=\sum_\alpha v_\alpha\Lambda_n(\mathsf v(\alpha))$. We introduce the Gaussian model
\begin{equation}
\label{e.gaussian_model_n}
    Z_b:=\sum_{\alpha\in\mathbb{N}^k}v_\alpha\int_{\mathbb{R}^n}\exp\left(\mathsf v(\alpha)\cdot x-\frac b2|x|^2\right)\frac{\mathrm{d} x}{(2\pi)^{n/2}},
\end{equation}
with Gibbs bracket $\left\langle\cdot\right\rangle_b$ on $\mathbb{R}^n\times\mathbb{N}^k$. Conditionally on $\alpha$, the coordinates $x_i$ are independent Gaussian random variables with mean $\mathsf v_i(\alpha)/b$ and variance $1/b$ under $\left\langle\cdot\right\rangle_b$, and integrating over $x$ gives $Z_b=\sum_\alpha v_\alpha\prod_{i\leqslant n}b^{-1/2}e^{\mathsf v_i(\alpha)^2/(2b)}$. In the notation of Appendix~\ref{s.app_cascade}, this is a discrete cascade tilted by $X(\Omega_\alpha):=\sum_{i\leqslant n}g(\mathsf v_i(\alpha))$ with $g(x)=x^2/(2b)$, a sum of identical functions of the marks of the $n$ coordinates. We collect the three facts about this tilted cascade that the proof uses.

First, by the additivity of the recursion, Lemma~\ref{l.tilted_cascade}, part~\eqref{i.tilted_additivity}, and by Step~1 of the proof of Lemma~\ref{l.scalar_initial_continuous_derivative}, in which the one-coordinate recursion was computed, we have
\begin{equation}
\label{e.gaussian_model_free_energy}
    \frac1n\mathbb{E}\log Z_b=\mathbb{E}\log Z^\circ_{a,b}(\rho)=\mathcal X_a(\rho,b)=\mathcal D^\circ_a(\rho,b)-\frac{b-1}2+\rho(1).
\end{equation}
Second, by Lemma~\ref{l.tilted_cascade}, part~\eqref{i.tilted_marks}, the marks $(\Omega_{\alpha,i})_{i\leqslant n}$ of the $n$ coordinates along the sampled leaf are independent and identically distributed under $\mathbb{E}\left\langle\cdot\right\rangle_b$, with a law that does not depend on $n$; since, conditionally on $\alpha$ and on the marks, the coordinate $x_i$ is Gaussian with a law that only depends on $\mathsf v_i(\alpha)$, the pairs $(\mathsf v_i(\alpha),x_i)_{i\leqslant n}$ are independent and identically distributed under $\mathbb{E}\left\langle\cdot\right\rangle_b$ as well, with a law $\nu$ that does not depend on $n$. Under $\nu$, all moments are finite, since the tilted path law in \eqref{e.tilted_path_law} is Gaussian, the tilts $X_j$ of the recursion being quadratic. Moreover, $b\mapsto\log Z_b$ is almost surely convex, with derivative $-\frac12\left\langle|x|^2\right\rangle_b$, so that the monotone convergence argument of Step~5 of the proof of Lemma~\ref{l.scalar_initial_continuous_derivative} shows that $b\mapsto\frac1n\mathbb{E}\log Z_b$ is differentiable with derivative $-\frac1{2n}\mathbb{E}\left\langle|x|^2\right\rangle_b=-\frac12\mathbb{E}\left\langle x_1^2\right\rangle_b$, by exchangeability. Comparing with~\eqref{e.gaussian_model_free_energy} and~\eqref{e.block_b_derivative}, we get $\mathbb{E}\left\langle x_1^2\right\rangle_b=\mathbb{E}\left\langle\tau^2\right\rangle^\circ_{\rho,b}$, which equals $1$ when $b=b_a(\rho)$, by~\eqref{e.scalar_initial_normalization}. For this value of $b$, the independence gives the law of large numbers
\begin{equation}
\label{e.radial_concentration_gaussian_model}
    \mathbb{E}\left\langle\left(\frac1n|x|^2-1\right)^2\right\rangle_{b_a(\rho)}=\frac1n\operatorname{Var}_\nu\left(x_1^2\right)=:\frac{C_0}n,
\end{equation}
where $C_0<\infty$ does not depend on $n$.

Third, by the variance bound of Lemma~\ref{l.tilted_cascade}, part~\eqref{i.tilted_variance}, applied to the same tilt, we have $\operatorname{Var}(\log Z_b)\leqslant Cn$; together with $|\mathbb{E}\log Z_b|=n|\mathcal X_a(\rho,b)|$, this gives
\begin{equation}
\label{e.log_Z_second_moment}
    \mathbb{E}\left[(\log Z_b)^2\right]\leqslant Cn^2,
\end{equation}
for a constant $C$ depending only on $\rho,a,b$.

We now write $x\in\mathbb{R}^n$ in polar coordinates, $x=r\sigma$ with $r:=|x|/\sqrt n\in[0,\infty)$ and $\sigma:=\sqrt n\,x/|x|\in\mathbb{S}_n$. The Lebesgue measure decomposes as $(2\pi)^{-n/2}\mathrm{d} x=\kappa_nr^{n-1}\mathrm{d} r\,\mu_n(\mathrm{d}\sigma)$, with
\begin{equation}
\label{e.kappa_n_def}
    \kappa_n:=\frac{2(n/2)^{n/2}}{\Gamma(n/2)},
    \qquad\text{so that}\qquad\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac1n\log\kappa_n=\frac12
\end{equation}
by Stirling's formula. Since $\mathsf v(\alpha)\cdot x=r\,\mathsf v(\alpha)\cdot\sigma$ and $|x|^2=nr^2$, we obtain
\begin{equation}
\label{e.Z_b_polar}
    Z_b=\int_0^\infty B(r)\,e^{-nbr^2/2}\kappa_nr^{n-1}\mathrm{d} r,
    \qquad
    B(r):=\sum_{\alpha}v_\alpha\Lambda_n\left(r\mathsf v(\alpha)\right).
\end{equation}
The function $B$ is nondecreasing, by the monotonicity of $r\mapsto\Lambda_n(rv)$ noted above, and $B(1)=A_n$. Under $\left\langle\cdot\right\rangle_b$, the radial variable $r$ has density $B(r)e^{-nbr^2/2}\kappa_nr^{n-1}/Z_b$. The identity~\eqref{e.Z_b_polar} expresses the Gaussian model as a mixture of spherical models with radius $r\sqrt n$; the multiplier $b_a(\rho)$ is the one for which this mixture concentrates near $r=1$.

\smallskip
\noindent\emph{Step 3: Lower bound on $\overline F^\circ_{n,a}(\rho)$.}\par
Let $\delta>0$. Restricting the integral in~\eqref{e.Z_b_polar} to $[1,1+\delta]$, and using $B(r)\geqslant B(1)=A_n$, $r^{n-1}\geqslant1$, and $b>0$ there, we obtain
\begin{equation*}
    Z_b\geqslant A_n\,\delta\kappa_n\exp\left(-\frac{nb(1+\delta)^2}2\right).
\end{equation*}
Taking logarithms and expectations, dividing by $n$, and using~\eqref{e.gaussian_model_free_energy} and~\eqref{e.kappa_n_def}, we get
\begin{equation*}
    \limsup_{n\to\infty}\left(\frac1n\mathbb{E}\log A_n-\rho(1)\right)\leqslant\mathcal X_a(\rho,b)-\rho(1)+\frac{b(1+\delta)^2}2-\frac12=\mathcal D^\circ_a(\rho,b)+\frac b2\left((1+\delta)^2-1\right).
\end{equation*}
Letting $\delta\to0$ and choosing $b=b_a(\rho)$, for which $\mathcal D^\circ_a(\rho,b)=-\psi^\circ_a(\rho)$, we obtain
\begin{equation}
\label{e.initial_lower_bound}
    \liminf_{n\to\infty}\overline F^\circ_{n,a}(\rho)\geqslant\psi^\circ_a(\rho).
\end{equation}

\smallskip
\noindent\emph{Step 4: Upper bound on $\overline F^\circ_{n,a}(\rho)$.}\par
We now fix $b:=b_a(\rho)$ and $\delta\in(0,\frac12)$. Since $|r-1|\leqslant|r^2-1|$ for $r\geqslant0$, Chebyshev's inequality gives $\left\langle\mathds{1}_{\{|r-1|>\delta\}}\right\rangle_b\leqslant\delta^{-2}\left\langle(r^2-1)^2\right\rangle_b$. Let $G$ be the event $\{\left\langle(r^2-1)^2\right\rangle_b\leqslant\delta^2/2\}$, whose complement has probability at most $2C_0/(n\delta^2)$ by~\eqref{e.radial_concentration_gaussian_model} and Markov's inequality. On $G$, the radial variable lies in $[1-\delta,1+\delta]$ with $\left\langle\cdot\right\rangle_b$-probability at least $\frac12$, so that, by~\eqref{e.Z_b_polar} and the monotonicity of $B$,
\begin{equation*}
    \frac{Z_b}2\leqslant\int_{1-\delta}^{1+\delta}B(r)e^{-nbr^2/2}\kappa_nr^{n-1}\mathrm{d} r\leqslant2\delta\,B(1+\delta)\,\kappa_n(1+\delta)^{n}e^{-nb(1-\delta)^2/2}.
\end{equation*}
Hence, on $G$,
\begin{equation}
\label{e.window_bound}
    \log B(1+\delta)\geqslant\log Z_b+D_n,
    \qquad D_n:=\frac{nb(1-\delta)^2}2-\log\kappa_n-n\log(1+\delta)-\log(4\delta),
\end{equation}
where $D_n$ is deterministic with $|D_n|\leqslant C_\delta n$. Outside $G$, we only use $\log B(1+\delta)\geqslant0$, which holds since $\Lambda_n\geqslant1$. Multiplying~\eqref{e.window_bound} by $\mathds{1}_G$ and taking expectations, we get
\begin{equation*}             
\mathbb{E}\log B(1+\delta)\geqslant\mathbb{E}\log Z_b-\mathbb{E}[|\log Z_b|\mathds{1}_{G^c}]-|D_n|\mathbb{P}(G^c)+D_n,
\end{equation*}
and by the Cauchy--Schwarz inequality and~\eqref{e.log_Z_second_moment},
\begin{equation*}
    \mathbb{E}\left[|\log Z_b|\mathds{1}_{G^c}\right]\leqslant\left(\mathbb{E}\left[(\log Z_b)^2\right]\right)^{1/2}\mathbb{P}(G^c)^{1/2}\leqslant C_\delta\sqrt n.
\end{equation*}
Therefore,
\begin{equation}
\label{e.window_bound_expectation}
    \mathbb{E}\log B(1+\delta)\geqslant\mathbb{E}\log Z_b+\frac{nb(1-\delta)^2}2-\log\kappa_n-n\log(1+\delta)-C_\delta\left(\sqrt n+1\right),
\end{equation}
where $C_\delta$ depends on $\delta$ and on $\rho,a$, but not on $n$. Finally, we relate $B(1+\delta)$ to the free energy. Since $(1+\delta)\mathsf v(\alpha)=\sqrt2(1+\delta)\mathsf w^\rho(\alpha)+(1+\delta)a$ and $(1+\delta)\mathsf w^\rho$ is the discrete field~\eqref{e.discrete_field} associated with the path $\rho_\delta:=(1+\delta)^2\rho$, we have $\mathbb{E}\log B(1+\delta)=n\rho_\delta(1)-n\overline F^\circ_{n,a_\delta}(\rho_\delta)$ with $a_\delta:=(1+\delta)a$, by~\eqref{e.equiv_cascade_fe}, and the Lipschitz bounds recorded below~\eqref{e.one_species_initial_F} give
\begin{equation*}
    \left|\overline F^\circ_{n,a_\delta}(\rho_\delta)-\overline F^\circ_{n,a}(\rho)\right|\leqslant(2\delta+\delta^2)|\rho|_{L^1}+\delta|a|.
\end{equation*}
Dividing~\eqref{e.window_bound_expectation} by $n$, inserting~\eqref{e.gaussian_model_free_energy} and~\eqref{e.kappa_n_def}, and letting $n\to\infty$, we arrive at
\begin{equation*}
    \liminf_{n\to\infty}\left(-\overline F^\circ_{n,a}(\rho)\right)\geqslant\mathcal D_a^\circ(\rho,b)-\frac b2\left(1-(1-\delta)^2\right)-\log(1+\delta)-\left((1+\delta)^2-1\right)\rho(1)-(2\delta+\delta^2)|\rho|_{L^1}-\delta|a|.
\end{equation*}
The right-hand side is $\mathcal D^\circ_a(\rho,b)+O(\delta)$ as $\delta\to0$, and $\mathcal D_a^\circ(\rho,b_a(\rho))=-\psi^\circ_a(\rho)$. Hence, we obtain that $\limsup_n\overline F^\circ_{n,a}(\rho)\leqslant\psi^\circ_a(\rho)$, which together with~\eqref{e.initial_lower_bound} proves~\eqref{e.one_species_limit}, and completes the proof.
<!-- end proof-10 -->
<!-- proposition-5: body_md -->
\label{p.crit_pt_bdd_spherical}
Assume that $\lambda_\infty\in\mathbb{Q}^{\mathscr{S}}$, let $M\in\mathbb{N}$ be such that $M_s:=M\lambda_{\infty,s}\in\mathbb{N}$ for every $s\in\mathscr{S}$, and consider the sequence of sizes
\begin{gather}
    N_n:=nM,
    \qquad
    |I_{N_n,s}|=nM_s,
    \qquad n\in\mathbb{N},
    \label{e.compatible_sequence}
\end{gather}
along which $\lambda_{N_n}=\lambda_\infty$. For every $t>0$ and $q\in\mathcal Q_{\infty,\uparrow}^{\mathscr{S}}$, there exists $p\in\mathcal Q_{\infty,\leqslant\lambda_\infty}^{\mathscr{S}}$ such that
\begin{gather}
    p=\partial_q\psi\left(q+t\nabla\xi(p)\right),
    \label{e.spherical_critical_relation}\\
    \limsup_{n\to\infty}\overline F_{N_n}(t,q)\leqslant\mathscr{P}_{t,q}(p).
    \label{e.spherical_critical_bounds}
\end{gather}
<!-- end proposition-5 -->
<!-- lemma-6: body_md -->
\label{l.inner_infimum}
Let $t\geqslant0$, $q\in\mathcal Q_\infty^{\mathscr{S}}$, and $p\in\mathcal Q_{\infty,\leqslant\lambda_\infty}^{\mathscr{S}}$, and set $\pi:=q+t\nabla\xi(p)\in\mathcal Q_\infty^{\mathscr{S}}$. If $p=\partial_q\psi(\pi)$, then
\begin{equation}
\label{e.inner_infimum}
    \inf_{q'\in\mathcal Q_\infty^{\mathscr{S}}}\mathcal J_{t,q}(q',p)=\mathcal J_{t,q}(\pi,p)=\mathscr{P}_{t,q}(p).
\end{equation}
<!-- end lemma-6 -->
<!-- proof-11: body_md -->
Let $q'\in\mathcal Q_\infty^{\mathscr{S}}$, and set $\kappa:=q'-\pi$, so that $\pi+\varepsilon\kappa=(1-\varepsilon)\pi+\varepsilon q'\in\mathcal Q_\infty^{\mathscr{S}}$ for $\varepsilon\in[0,1]$. By the convexity of $\psi$ (Lemma~\ref{l.psi_convex}),
\begin{equation}
\label{e.supporting_hyperplane}
    \psi(q')-\psi(\pi)\geqslant\lim_{\varepsilon\searrow0}\frac{\psi(\pi+\varepsilon\kappa)-\psi(\pi)}{\varepsilon}=\left\langle q'-\pi,\partial_q\psi(\pi)\right\rangle_{L^2}.
\end{equation}
With $p=\partial_q\psi(\pi)$, it reads $\psi(q')-\left\langle q',p\right\rangle_{L^2}\geqslant\psi(\pi)-\left\langle\pi,p\right\rangle_{L^2}$, and adding $\left\langle q,p\right\rangle_{L^2}+t\int_0^1\xi(p(r))\mathrm{d} r$ to both sides yields $\mathcal J_{t,q}(q',p)\geqslant\mathcal J_{t,q}(\pi,p)$. Since $\pi\in\mathcal Q_\infty^{\mathscr{S}}$ is itself an admissible competitor, the infimum in~\eqref{e.inner_infimum} equals $\mathcal J_{t,q}(\pi,p)$, and the second equality in~\eqref{e.inner_infimum} is the identity noted after~\eqref{e.spherical_Parisi_functional}.
<!-- end proof-11 -->
<!-- remark-2: body_md -->
\label{r.linear_form_hamiltonians}
The Hamiltonian $H^{x,y,q}_N$ depends on the cascade variable $\alpha$ only through the cascade fields $w^{q^s}_i(\alpha)$ and the fields $w^{\mathsf h,j}_e(\alpha)$ of the construction~\eqref{e.feature_field_construction}, and it is linear in these fields, with coefficients that are polynomials in~$\sigma$; this remains true of its radial derivatives, hence of $V^{x,y,q}_N$. It is therefore of the form~\eqref{e.linear_cascade_hamiltonian} considered in Appendix~\ref{s.app_concentration}, with the finite family of the cascade fields and the countable family of the perturbation fields. The tail condition~\eqref{e.linear_cascade_tail} holds by~\eqref{e.ch_perturbation_lipschitz_summability}, since the contribution to the variance of the indices $\mathsf h$ outside a finite set $F$ is at most $CN\eta_N^2\sum_{\mathsf h\notin F}c_{\mathsf h}^2\Lambda_{\mathsf h}$, for some constant $C<\infty$. The same applies to the bulk Hamiltonian $\widetilde H^{x,y,q}_N$ of Subsection~\ref{s.bulk_and_chart_expansion} and to the Hamiltonian of the $(N+M)$-spin system. The invariance~\eqref{e.invariance_cascade} is stated for finitely many fields; we apply it to the Hamiltonian in which the sum over $\mathsf h$ is restricted to a finite set $F$, conditionally on the fields that do not depend on the cascade, and we then let $F$ increase to $\mathbb{N}^4$, using Lemma~\ref{l.gaussian_comparison_covariance_norm} below: by the Cauchy--Schwarz inequality, the covariances of the restricted and unrestricted Hamiltonians differ by at most the bound on the variance just given. Consequently, for every $n\in\mathbb{N}$, the overlap array $(\alpha^\ell\wedge\alpha^{\ell'})_{\ell,\ell'\leqslant n}$ of $n$ replicas has the same law under every Gibbs measure built from these Hamiltonians as under $\mathbb{E}\left\langle\cdot\right\rangle_\mathfrak{R}$; in particular, the overlap $\alpha\wedge\alpha'$ of two replicas is uniformly distributed on $[0,1]$. Moreover, the corresponding free energies concentrate around their expectations at the rate given by Lemma~\ref{l.cascade_concentration}. These two facts are used repeatedly below without further comment.
<!-- end remark-2 -->
<!-- lemma-7: body_md -->
\label{l.comput_cov_radial}
Let $f=f(v,u)$ be a function which is smooth in $v$ on a neighborhood of $\{(\sqrt{r^sr'^s}v_s)_{s\in\mathscr{S}}:r,r'\in U_0,\ |v_s|\leqslant\lambda_s\}$, and let $\mathsf W$ be a centered Gaussian field on $\{S_r\sigma:r\in U_0,\ \sigma\in\Sigma_N\}\times\mathfrak U$ with covariance $\mathbb{E}\mathsf W(\sigma,\alpha)\mathsf W(\sigma',\alpha')=f(R_N(\sigma,\sigma'),\alpha\wedge\alpha')$. For $\eta>0$ and $y\in\mathbb{R}^{\mathscr{S}}$, set
\begin{align*}
    \mathsf W^y(\sigma,\alpha):= \mathsf W(\sigma,\alpha) + 2\eta\sum_{s\in\mathscr{S}}y^s\partial_{r^s}\mathsf W(S_r\sigma,\alpha)\big|_{r=\vec{\mathbf{1}}},
    \qquad \sigma\in\Sigma_N.
\end{align*}
Then $\mathbb{E} \mathsf W^y(\sigma,\alpha)\mathsf W^y(\sigma',\alpha') = f_{\eta,y}(R_N(\sigma,\sigma'),\alpha\wedge\alpha')$, where
\begin{align}\label{e.f_eta_N,y=}
    f_{\eta,y}(v,u):=f(v,u)+2\eta\,\mathsf D_yf(v,u)+\eta^2\mathsf D_y^2f(v,u).
\end{align}
<!-- end lemma-7 -->
<!-- proof-12: body_md -->
Set $v:=R_N(\sigma,\sigma')$ and $u:=\alpha\wedge\alpha'$. By~\eqref{e.overlap_dilation}, the covariance of $\mathsf W(S_r\sigma,\alpha)$ and $\mathsf W(S_{r'}\sigma',\alpha')$ is $f((\sqrt{r^sr'^s}v_s)_{s\in\mathscr{S}},u)$. Since radial derivatives are $L^2$ derivatives, they commute with expectations, and
\begin{align*}
    \mathbb{E}\mathsf W^y(\sigma,\alpha)\mathsf W^y(\sigma',\alpha')={}&\left(1+2\eta\sum_{s\in\mathscr{S}}y^s\partial_{r^s}\right)\left(1+2\eta\sum_{s\in\mathscr{S}}y^s\partial_{r'^s}\right)f\left((\sqrt{r^sr'^s}\,v_s)_{s\in\mathscr{S}},u\right)\Big|_{r=r'=\vec{\mathbf{1}}}.
\end{align*}
By the chain rule, $2\partial_{r^s}f((\sqrt{r^sr'^s}v_s)_s,u)|_{r=\vec{\mathbf{1}}}=v_s\partial_{v_s}f((\sqrt{r'^s}v_s)_s,u)$, and similarly for $r'$. Expanding the product of the two operators gives~\eqref{e.f_eta_N,y=}.
<!-- end proof-12 -->
<!-- lemma-8: body_md -->
\label{l.block_disintegration}
For every measurable function $f:\mathbb{S}_{n+m}\to[0,\infty)$, we have
\begin{align}
    \int_{\mathbb{S}_{n+m}}f(\rho)\,\mu_{n+m}(\mathrm{d}\rho)
    =\iint_{\mathbb{S}_n\times \mathcal B_{m,n}}f\left(\phi_{m,n}(\sigma,\tau)\right)
    p_{m,n}(\tau)\,\mathrm{d}\tau\,\mu_n(\mathrm{d}\sigma).
    \label{e.block_disintegration}
\end{align}
Moreover, for each fixed $m$, the density $p_{m,n}$ converges to the density of $\boldsymbol{\gamma}_m$ locally uniformly on $\mathbb{R}^m$ as $n\to\infty$.
<!-- end lemma-8 -->
<!-- proof-13: body_md -->
Set $R:=\sqrt{n+m}$, and parametrize $\mathbb{S}_{n+m}$ minus a null set by
\begin{equation*}
    \mathcal B_{m,n}\times\{\omega\in\mathbb{R}^n:|\omega|=1\}\ni(\tau,\omega)\longmapsto\left(\sqrt{R^2-|\tau|^2}\,\omega,\tau\right).
\end{equation*}
The partial derivative of this map with respect to $\tau_k$ is $(-\tau_k(R^2-|\tau|^2)^{-1/2}\omega,e_k)$, and its differential in a unit direction $\zeta$ tangent to the sphere at $\omega$ is $((R^2-|\tau|^2)^{1/2}\zeta,0)$. Each vector of the second kind is orthogonal to each vector of the first kind, since $\zeta\perp\omega$. The Gram determinant of the $m$ vectors of the first kind is $\det(I_m+\tau\tau^\intercal/(R^2-|\tau|^2))=R^2/(R^2-|\tau|^2)$, and that of the $n-1$ vectors of the second kind, with $\zeta$ ranging over an orthonormal basis of the tangent space, is $(R^2-|\tau|^2)^{n-1}$. Denoting by $\omega_{n-1}$ the surface measure on the unit sphere of $\mathbb{R}^n$, and taking the square root of the product of these two determinants, we find that the surface measure on $\mathbb{S}_{n+m}$ is
\begin{equation*}
    R\left(R^2-|\tau|^2\right)^{\frac{n-2}{2}}\mathrm{d}\tau\,\omega_{n-1}(\mathrm{d}\omega)
\end{equation*}
in these coordinates. Normalizing this measure, we see that under $\mu_{n+m}$, the marginal law of $\tau$ has a density proportional to $(1-|\tau|^2/(n+m))^{n/2-1}$ on $\mathcal B_{m,n}$ and that, conditionally on $\tau$, the vector $\omega$ is uniform on the unit sphere of $\mathbb{R}^n$; equivalently, $\sigma:=\sqrt n\,\omega$ is distributed according to $\mu_n$, and the first $n$ coordinates of $\rho$ are $\sqrt{(n+m-|\tau|^2)/n}\,\sigma$. This is the content of~\eqref{e.block_disintegration}, up to the identification of the normalizing constant, which follows from the classical formula
\begin{equation*}
    \int_{\{|v|<1\}}\left(1-|v|^2\right)^{a-1}\mathrm{d} v=\frac{\pi^{m/2}\Gamma(a)}{\Gamma(a+\frac m2)},
    \qquad a>0,
\end{equation*}
applied with $a=n/2$ after the change of variables $\tau=Rv$. For the last assertion, Stirling's formula gives $\Gamma(\frac{n+m}2)/\Gamma(\frac n2)=(\frac n2)^{m/2}(1+o(1))$ as $n\to\infty$, so that the constant in~\eqref{e.block_density} converges to $(2\pi)^{-m/2}$, while $(1-|\tau|^2/(n+m))^{n/2-1}$ converges to $e^{-|\tau|^2/2}$ uniformly on compact sets.
<!-- end proof-13 -->
<!-- lemma-9: body_md -->
\label{l.gaussian_comparison_covariance_norm}
Let $\mathsf P$ be a probability measure on a measurable space $\mathbb X$, and let $\mathsf W^0$ and $\mathsf W^1$ be Gaussian fields indexed by $\mathbb X$, with bounded means $m^0$, $m^1$ and bounded covariances $C^0$, $C^1$. Set $Z^i:=\int_{\mathbb X}e^{\mathsf W^i(\mathsf x)}\mathsf P(\mathrm{d}\mathsf x)$, and let $\left\langle\cdot\right\rangle_i$ be the associated Gibbs bracket, for $i\in\{0,1\}$. Then
\begin{equation*}
    \left|\mathbb{E}\log Z^1-\mathbb{E}\log Z^0\right|\leqslant\sup_{\mathbb X}\left|m^1-m^0\right|+\sup_{\mathbb X\times\mathbb X}\left|C^1-C^0\right|,
\end{equation*}
and, for every $n\in\mathbb{N}$, there is a constant $C_n<\infty$, depending only on $n$, such that, for every bounded measurable function $f$ of $n$ replicas,
\begin{equation*}
    \left|\mathbb{E}\left\langle f\right\rangle_1-\mathbb{E}\left\langle f\right\rangle_0\right|\leqslant C_n\|f\|_\infty\left(\sup_{\mathbb X}\left|m^1-m^0\right|+\sup_{\mathbb X\times\mathbb X}\left|C^1-C^0\right|\right).
\end{equation*}
In particular, with the notation~\eqref{e.Gaussian_approx}, if $\mathsf W^0_N\stackrel{\delta_N,\delta'_N}{\mathrel{\hstretch{1.8}{\approx}}}\mathsf W^1_N$ uniformly over $\mathbb X_N$, then
\begin{align*}
    \mathbb{E}\log Z^0_N\stackrel{\delta_N+\delta'_N}{\mathrel{\hstretch{1.8}{\approx}}}\mathbb{E}\log Z^1_N
    \qquad\text{and}\qquad
    \mathbb{E}\left\langle f\right\rangle_{0,N}\stackrel{\delta_N+\delta'_N}{\mathrel{\hstretch{1.8}{\approx}}} \mathbb{E}\left\langle f\right\rangle_{1,N}.
\end{align*}
<!-- end lemma-9 -->
<!-- proof-14: body_md -->
Let $\mathsf G^i:=\mathsf W^i-m^i$, and realize $\mathsf G^0$ and $\mathsf G^1$ as independent fields; this does not change the law of $Z^0$, of $Z^1$, nor of the individual brackets. For $u\in[0,1]$, set $\mathsf W^u:=(1-u)m^0+um^1+\sqrt{1-u}\,\mathsf G^0+\sqrt u\,\mathsf G^1$, and let $Z^u$ and $\left\langle\cdot\right\rangle_u$ be the associated partition function and bracket. Gaussian integration by parts gives
\begin{equation*}
    \frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d} u}\mathbb{E}\log Z^u=\mathbb{E}\left\langle m^1(\mathsf x)-m^0(\mathsf x)\right\rangle_u+\frac12\mathbb{E}\left\langle (C^1-C^0)(\mathsf x,\mathsf x)\right\rangle_u-\frac12\mathbb{E}\left\langle(C^1-C^0)(\mathsf x,\mathsf x')\right\rangle_u,
\end{equation*}
where $\mathsf x,\mathsf x'$ denote two replicas, and the first estimate follows by integration over $u\in[0,1]$. Similarly, $\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d} u}\mathbb{E}\left\langle f\right\rangle_u$ is a finite sum of Gibbs averages of products of $f$ with $(m^1-m^0)(\mathsf x^\ell)$ or $(C^1-C^0)(\mathsf x^\ell,\mathsf x^{\ell'})$, for $\ell,\ell'\leqslant n+2$, with coefficients depending only on $n$; this gives the second estimate. The last assertion is a restatement of the first two.
<!-- end proof-14 -->
<!-- lemma-10: body_md -->
\label{l.quadratically_confined_Gaussian_comparison}
For every $C_0<\infty$ and $M\in\mathbb{N}$, the following holds. Let $\mu^0$ be a probability measure on a measurable space $\mathbb X^0$, let $B\subseteq\mathbb{R}^M$ be a bounded measurable set, let $\nu$ be a probability measure on $B$ with $\int|\tau|^2\nu(\mathrm{d}\tau)=M$, and set $\mathbb X:=\mathbb X^0\times B$ and $\mu:=\mu^0\otimes\nu$. Let $\mathsf W^0$ and $\mathsf W^1$ be Gaussian fields indexed by $\mathsf z=(\mathsf z_0,\tau)\in\mathbb X$, with means $m^0$, $m^1$ and covariances $C^0$, $C^1$, such that $\mathsf W^0(\mathsf z_0,\tau)$ does not depend on $\tau$, $m^0$ and $C^0$ are bounded, and
\begin{equation}
    |m^1(\mathsf z)-m^0(\mathsf z)|+|C^1(\mathsf z,\mathsf z')-C^0(\mathsf z,\mathsf z')|\leqslant C_0\left(1+|\tau|^2+|\tau'|^2\right),
    \qquad \mathsf z,\mathsf z'\in\mathbb X.
    \label{e.quadratic_kernel_comparison}
\end{equation}
Let $Z^i:=\int_{\mathbb X}e^{\mathsf W^i(\mathsf z)}\mu(\mathrm{d}\mathsf z)$ for $i\in\{0,1\}$, and let $\left\langle\cdot\right\rangle_1$ be the Gibbs bracket associated with $Z^1$. If
\begin{equation}
    \mathbb{E}\left\langle|\tau|^2\right\rangle_1=M,
    \label{e.quadratic_comparison_second_moments}
\end{equation}
then $|\mathbb{E}\log Z^1-\mathbb{E}\log Z^0|\leqslant 3C_0(1+M)$.
<!-- end lemma-10 -->
<!-- proof-15: body_md -->
Since $B$, $m^0$, and $C^0$ are bounded, the fields have bounded means and variances on $\mathbb X$, so that $Z^0$ and $Z^1$ are almost surely finite with integrable logarithms. As in the previous proof, we take the centered fields $\mathsf G^i:=\mathsf W^i-m^i$ to be independent. For $u\in[0,1]$ and $c\geqslant0$, we consider the interpolation with a quadratic confinement,
\begin{equation*}
    \Phi(u,c):=\mathbb{E}\log\int_{\mathbb X}\exp\left((1-u)m^0(\mathsf z)+um^1(\mathsf z)+\sqrt{1-u}\,\mathsf G^0(\mathsf z)+\sqrt u\,\mathsf G^1(\mathsf z)-c|\tau|^2\right)\mu(\mathrm{d}\mathsf z),
\end{equation*}
and we denote by $\left\langle\cdot\right\rangle_{u,c}$ the associated Gibbs bracket. Gaussian integration by parts, as in the previous proof, together with~\eqref{e.quadratic_kernel_comparison}, gives
\begin{equation}
    \left|\partial_u\Phi(u,c)\right|\leqslant 3C_0\left(1+\mathbb{E}\left\langle|\tau|^2\right\rangle_{u,c}\right)\qquad\text{and}\qquad \partial_c\Phi(u,c)=-\mathbb{E}\left\langle|\tau|^2\right\rangle_{u,c}.
    \label{e.confined_interpolation_derivatives}
\end{equation}
Set $c_0:=3C_0$. Along the path $u\mapsto(u,c_0(1-u))$, we obtain from~\eqref{e.confined_interpolation_derivatives} that
\begin{equation*}
    \frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d} u}\Phi\left(u,c_0(1-u)\right)=\partial_u\Phi+c_0\mathbb{E}\left\langle|\tau|^2\right\rangle_{u,c_0(1-u)}\geqslant-3C_0.
\end{equation*}
Moreover, since $\mathsf W^0$ does not depend on $\tau$ and $\mu$ is a product measure, Jensen's inequality and the assumption on $\nu$ give
\begin{equation*}
    \Phi(0,c_0)-\Phi(0,0)=\log\int_Be^{-c_0|\tau|^2}\nu(\mathrm{d}\tau)\geqslant-c_0M.
\end{equation*}
Combining the last two displays yields $\mathbb{E}\log Z^1=\Phi(1,0)\geqslant\Phi(0,c_0)-3C_0\geqslant\mathbb{E}\log Z^0-c_0M-3C_0$. For the reverse inequality, we use the path $u\mapsto(u,c_0u)$, along which~\eqref{e.confined_interpolation_derivatives} gives $\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d} u}\Phi(u,c_0u)\leqslant3C_0$, so that $\Phi(1,c_0)\leqslant\Phi(0,0)+3C_0$. By Jensen's inequality and~\eqref{e.quadratic_comparison_second_moments},
\begin{equation*}
    \Phi(1,0)-\Phi(1,c_0)=\mathbb{E}\left[-\log\left\langle e^{-c_0|\tau|^2}\right\rangle_{1}\right]\leqslant c_0\mathbb{E}\left\langle|\tau|^2\right\rangle_{1}=c_0M.
\end{equation*}
Hence $\mathbb{E}\log Z^1=\Phi(1,0)\leqslant\mathbb{E}\log Z^0+3C_0+c_0M$, which completes the proof.
<!-- end proof-15 -->
<!-- lemma-11: body_md -->
\label{l.fixed_block_increment_bound}
There exists a constant $C<\infty$ such that, for every sufficiently large $N$,
\begin{equation*}
    \sup_{x,y,q}|A_N(x,y,q)|\leqslant C.
\end{equation*}
<!-- end lemma-11 -->
<!-- proof-16: body_md -->
The Hamiltonian $H_{N+M}^{x,y,q}$ of the $(N+M)$-spin system is built with the coefficient $\eta_{N+M}$, whereas $H_N^{x,y,q}$ is built with $\eta_N$. We first compare $H_N^{x,y,q}$ with a version of the $(N+M)$-spin Hamiltonian built with $\eta_N$, and then return to $\eta_{N+M}$.

\smallskip
\noindent\emph{Step 1: Overlaps in the chart.}\par
Let $\rho=(S_{r_N(\tau)}\sigma,\tau)$ and $\rho'=(S_{r_N(\tau')}\sigma',\tau')$ with $(\sigma,\tau),(\sigma',\tau')\in\Sigma_N\times\mathcal B_N$. By~\eqref{e.R_Ns_def}, \eqref{e.overlap_dilation}, and~\eqref{e.radial_factor},
\begin{equation}
    R_{N+M,s}(\rho,\rho')=\frac{N}{N+M}\sqrt{r_N^s(\tau)r_N^s(\tau')}\,R_{N,s}(\sigma,\sigma')+\frac{1}{N+M}\sum_{j\in\mathsf M_s}\tau_j\tau_j'.
    \label{e.full_and_bulk_overlap_identity}
\end{equation}
Since $|\sqrt a-1|\leqslant|a-1|$ for $a\geqslant0$ and $0<r_N^s(\tau)\leqslant2$, we have $|\sqrt{r_N^s(\tau)r_N^s(\tau')}-1|\leqslant2(|r_N^s(\tau)-1|+|r_N^s(\tau')-1|)$, and $N|r^s_N(\tau)-1|\leqslant(M_s+|\tau^{(s)}|^2)/\lambda_s$ by~\eqref{e.radial_factor} and~\eqref{e.N_compatible_block}. Using also $|R_{N,s}(\sigma,\sigma')|\leqslant\lambda_s$, we deduce from~\eqref{e.full_and_bulk_overlap_identity} that
\begin{equation}
    (N+M)\left|R_{N+M}(\rho,\rho')-R_N(\sigma,\sigma')\right|\leqslant C\left(1+|\tau|^2+|\tau'|^2\right),
    \label{e.full_and_bulk_overlap_bound}
\end{equation}
for a constant $C$ depending only on $M$.

\smallskip
\noindent\emph{Step 2: The $(N+M)$-spin system with coefficient $\eta_N$.}\par
For $K\in\{N,N+M\}$, let $\widehat H_{K;N}^{x,y,q}$ be defined as $H_K^{x,y,q}$ in~\eqref{e.perturbed_enriched_H} and~\eqref{e.full_radial_perturbation}, except that $\eta_K$ is replaced by $\eta_N$ throughout, and let $\widehat Z_{K;N}^{x,y,q}$ be the associated partition function. Thus $\widehat H_{N;N}^{x,y,q}=H_N^{x,y,q}$. The mean and covariance of $\widehat H_{K;N}^{x,y,q}$ are given by~\eqref{e.mean_perturbed_H} and~\eqref{e.covariance_perturbed_H}, with $N$ replaced by $K$ in the prefactors and in the overlaps, and with $\eta_N$ unchanged; we use here that $\lambda_K=\lambda$ by~\eqref{e.lambda_N_equals_lambda}.

Let $\rho,\rho'$ be as in Step~1. We claim that
\begin{equation}
    \Big|\mathbb{E}\widehat H_{N+M;N}^{x,y,q}(\rho,\alpha)-\mathbb{E} H_N^{x,y,q}(\sigma,\alpha)\Big|\leqslant C\left(1+|\tau|^2\right)
    \label{e.frozen_chart_mean_bound}
\end{equation}
and
\begin{multline}
    \Big|\operatorname{Cov}\left(\widehat H_{N+M;N}^{x,y,q}(\rho,\alpha),\widehat H_{N+M;N}^{x,y,q}(\rho',\alpha')\right)-\operatorname{Cov}\left(H_N^{x,y,q}(\sigma,\alpha),H_N^{x,y,q}(\sigma',\alpha')\right)\Big|\\
    \leqslant C\left(1+|\tau|^2+|\tau'|^2\right),
    \label{e.frozen_chart_covariance_bound}
\end{multline}
uniformly over $x,y,q$, $\alpha,\alpha'\in\mathfrak U$, and the configurations. For~\eqref{e.frozen_chart_mean_bound}, the first two terms in~\eqref{e.mean_perturbed_H} are proportional to $K$ with bounded coefficients, so the difference of their values at $K=N+M$ and $K=N$ is bounded by $CM$. For the external-field term, we note that $(S_{r_N(\tau)}\sigma)_i=\sqrt{r_N^s(\tau)}\sigma_i$ for $i\in I_{N,s}$, and that
\begin{equation*}
    \Big|\Big(\sqrt{r_N^s(\tau)}-1\Big)\sum_{i\in I_{N,s}}\sigma_i\Big|\leqslant N_s\left|r_N^s(\tau)-1\right|\leqslant M_s+|\tau^{(s)}|^2,
    \qquad
    \Big|\sum_{j\in\mathsf M_s}\tau_j\Big|\leqslant\sqrt{M_s}\,|\tau^{(s)}|,
\end{equation*}
by the Cauchy--Schwarz inequality and~\eqref{e.radial_factor}. This proves~\eqref{e.frozen_chart_mean_bound}. For~\eqref{e.frozen_chart_covariance_bound}, each term in~\eqref{e.covariance_perturbed_H} is of the form $Kg(R_K,u)$, where $g$ is one of the kernels $2t\xi_{\eta_N,y}$, $2\sum_s(1+\eta_Ny^s)^2q^s(u)v_s$, and $\eta_N^2\sum_{\mathsf h}x^2_{\mathsf h}c_{\mathsf h}^2(\mathsf C_{\mathsf h})_{\eta_N,y}$, and $R_K$ stands for $R_{N+M}(\rho,\rho')$ or $R_N(\sigma,\sigma')$. These kernels and their gradients in $v$ are bounded uniformly over $x,y,q$ on the range of overlaps, by the remark following~\eqref{e.mean_perturbed_H}. Writing
\begin{equation*}
    (N+M)g(R_{N+M},u)-Ng(R_N,u)=Mg(R_{N+M},u)+N\left(g(R_{N+M},u)-g(R_N,u)\right)
\end{equation*}
and using~\eqref{e.full_and_bulk_overlap_bound} for the second term proves~\eqref{e.frozen_chart_covariance_bound}.

We now apply Lemma~\ref{l.quadratically_confined_Gaussian_comparison} with $\mathbb X^0:=\Sigma_N\times\mathfrak U$, $\mu^0:=P_N\otimes\mathfrak{R}$, $B:=\mathcal B_N$, $\nu:=p_N^{\mathrm{ch}}(\tau)\mathrm{d}\tau$, and the fields
\begin{equation*}
    \mathsf W^0(\sigma,\tau,\alpha):=H_N^{x,y,q}(\sigma,\alpha),
    \qquad
    \mathsf W^1(\sigma,\tau,\alpha):=\widehat H_{N+M;N}^{x,y,q}\left((S_{r_N(\tau)}\sigma,\tau),\alpha\right).
\end{equation*}
The set $\mathcal B_N$ is bounded, $\nu$ is a probability measure on $\mathcal B_N$ with second moment $M$ by~\eqref{e.chart_second_moment}, and~\eqref{e.quadratic_kernel_comparison} holds by~\eqref{e.frozen_chart_mean_bound} and~\eqref{e.frozen_chart_covariance_bound}. By~\eqref{e.product_disintegration}, we have $Z^0=Z_N^{x,y,q}$ and $Z^1=\widehat Z_{N+M;N}^{x,y,q}$, and the bracket $\left\langle\cdot\right\rangle_1$ is the Gibbs bracket of $\widehat H_{N+M;N}^{x,y,q}$ expressed in the chart. It remains to verify~\eqref{e.quadratic_comparison_second_moments}. The mean and covariance of $\widehat H^{x,y,q}_{N+M;N}$ depend on the configurations only through their species overlaps and the sums $\sum_{i\in I_{N+M,s}}\rho_i$, which are invariant under permutations of the coordinates within each species. The law of the field is therefore invariant under such permutations, and so is $\mathbb{E}\left\langle\rho_i^2\right\rangle_1$ as a function of $i\in I_{N+M,s}$. Since $\sum_{i\in I_{N+M,s}}\rho_i^2=N_s+M_s$ on $\Sigma_{N+M}$, we get $\mathbb{E}\left\langle\rho_i^2\right\rangle_1=1$ for every $i$, hence $\mathbb{E}\left\langle|\tau^{(s)}|^2\right\rangle_1=M_s$ and $\mathbb{E}\left\langle|\tau|^2\right\rangle_1=M$. Lemma~\ref{l.quadratically_confined_Gaussian_comparison} thus yields
\begin{equation}
    \sup_{x,y,q}\left|\mathbb{E}\log\widehat Z_{N+M;N}^{x,y,q}-\mathbb{E}\log Z_N^{x,y,q}\right|\leqslant C.
    \label{e.frozen_fixed_block_increment}
\end{equation}

\smallskip
\noindent\emph{Step 3: Back to the coefficient $\eta_{N+M}$.}\par
Set $K:=N+M$. The fields $H_K^{x,y,q}$ and $\widehat H_{K;N}^{x,y,q}$ are built from the same Gaussian fields $H_K$, $W_K^q$, and $(H_K^{\mathsf h})_{\mathsf h}$; they differ only in that $\eta_K$ is replaced by $\eta_N$. By~\eqref{e.mean_perturbed_H}, their means differ by
\begin{equation*}
    (\eta_K-\eta_N)\Big(-2Kt\mathsf D_y\xi(\lambda)-2K\sum_{s\in\mathscr{S}}q^s(1)\lambda_sy^s+\sum_{s\in\mathscr{S}}h^sy^s\sum_{i\in I_{K,s}}\rho_i\Big),
\end{equation*}
which is bounded by $CK|\eta_K-\eta_N|$ in absolute value. By~\eqref{e.f_eta_N,y=}, for every kernel $f$,
\begin{equation*}
    f_{\eta_K,y}-f_{\eta_N,y}=(\eta_K-\eta_N)\left(2\mathsf D_yf+(\eta_K+\eta_N)\mathsf D_y^2f\right),
\end{equation*}
and $|\eta_K^2-\eta_N^2|\leqslant2|\eta_K-\eta_N|$. Applying this to the three terms in~\eqref{e.covariance_perturbed_H}, and using~\eqref{e.ch_perturbation_lipschitz_summability} to sum over $\mathsf h$, we find that the covariances of $H_K^{x,y,q}$ and $\widehat H_{K;N}^{x,y,q}$ differ by at most $CK|\eta_K-\eta_N|$, uniformly over $x,y,q$ and over $\Sigma_K\times\mathfrak U$. Lemma~\ref{l.gaussian_comparison_covariance_norm} therefore gives
\begin{equation}
    \sup_{x,y,q}\left|\mathbb{E}\log Z_{N+M}^{x,y,q}-\mathbb{E}\log\widehat Z_{N+M;N}^{x,y,q}\right|\leqslant CN|\eta_{N+M}-\eta_N|,
    \label{e.actual_and_frozen_increment}
\end{equation}
and the right-hand side tends to zero, since $N|\eta_{N+M}-\eta_N|\leqslant MN^{-1/16}$ by~\eqref{e.eta_N_def}. Combining~\eqref{e.ASS_increment_def}, \eqref{e.frozen_fixed_block_increment}, and~\eqref{e.actual_and_frozen_increment} proves the lemma.
